speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, February 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 82, to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
Grain

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have read carefully, Mr. Speaker, your remarks at the conclusion of my address last night and I want to say that, as usual, you are absolutely fair and correct. Your assistants found it necessary to call me to order when you were absent from the chamber and they, too, were quite correct and fair. But in my defence I should like to say that members supporting the government had been so far from this subject that I felt without some reference to some of the remarks made it would have been interpreted that we accepted those views. I have discussed the remarks I propose to make this morning with my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and I will try to be absolutely on the beam all the way.
We are discussing Bill 82, which is an act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain. I am against that all the way. We do not want credit. We have had too much credit. We want to get fair consideration, nothing more and nothing less. This -is not a temporary situation. While the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has not taken any part in this debate I want to call him as my witness in saying that this is not a temporary situation. The Minister of Finance, speaking in New York, quite correctly said that this situation has been caused by policies in other countries. He also said that his government, the government of Canada, is concerned about the fact that wheat production is the principal source of cash income to the great majority of western farmers and his government was bound to be greatly influenced by anything so vital to them and to the whole national economy.
I want to make an appeal to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The Prime Minister has established, and has earned, the respect of a great many Canadians. I feel it is not fair for him to be in a position where the two senior members of his cabinet are so irresponsible in discussing this national problem. The Prime Minister is still the chief, and with all due respect to the contribution the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made in the past

and I am among the first to give him credit for the outstanding job he did during the war-if he were to approach this problem as he did his problems during the war, he would be saying the same sort of thing that the Minister of Finance is saying, that this is not a problem which has resulted from beneficent nature. It is a problem which results from policies which are not formed outside of Canada.

Grain
If we had had as minister of agriculture during the war a man who approached this problem as did the minister of munitions and supply at that time, our present Minister of Trade and Commerce, our farmers would not be in the position where they are so bitter as they are now. Therefore, I suggest to the Prime Minister that he deal with this problem in two stages; that he persuade his two senior members to take a holiday right now and go to Florida and have the Minister of Finance pilot this bill through the house, because I am sure the Minister of Finance would say that this is not a temporary problem. He would admit that it is a problem, and I am sure the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), whom we are glad to see back in the house this morning, would do as he did last summer, namely, take over agriculture during the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, and he would certainly do a much better job than the Minister of Agriculture in getting this piece of legislation discussed. I am sure that with the two senior members out of the country the cabinet would be prepared to accept the analysis made by the Minister of Finance in New York.
The farmers do not want too much. They merely want recognition of the facts as they exist and an indication that the government is prepared to do something about them. After having taken that step, the logical step that would follow would be for both ministers to see that parliament got on well without them and they would tender their resignations, and we would be able to proceed from there on.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that over the weekend he should take a look at what his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, said during this debate. I wish to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no bitterness on my part as a result of the interjections of the Minister of Trade and Commerce last night. While I was speaking and giving him credit for supplying me with certain information, the Minister of Trade and Commerce interrupted by saying, as reported at page 1275 of Hansard:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has supplied you with nothing.
I accepted that and made my apologies, and later on at page 1276 of Hansard the minister said:
I would not furnish you with a postage stamp. That is all right. I suggest the Prime Minister have a look at the editorial in this morning's Globe and Mail having reference to the remarks made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am not going to read the editorial, Mr. Speaker. I merely ask the Prime Minister to read it and decide whether or

not it is in the interests of good government in Canada to have his minister suggesting while one of his colleagues, the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), was speaking that this should not be degenerating to a debate. I think the Prime Minister would agree that the statements made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce are subjects for debate and that members of the opposition in all parties should not be muzzled. Either this bill is worth debating and contains certain principles, or it is not. The Prime Minister should look at it.
It is also suggested that he review the performance of the second senior minister, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I am indebted to Judith Robinson for her analysis of the barter proposals of the Minister of Agriculture. While the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) says that there is no marketing problem, that there is no problem facing the farmers of Canada, at that very moment his colleague is negotiating a barter deal with Great Britain to exchange wheat for British immigrants. I am sure that everyone who has come to Canada in the last 50 years from any country will resent very much the proposal that we should now consider bartering human beings in order to get rid of a surplus of wheat which the Minister of Trade and Commerce says does not exist.

they come back to the bill and say, "We are going to be for or against this measure which has to do with loans."

Then the hon. member should have returned to a discussion which was relevant to the bill.
I will be at a loss in directing the discussion on a bill of this kind if the position of farmers over the years or at the present time in the economy of Canada is to be relevant to the discussion. I suggest to the Prime Minister that he take time over the weekend to read Judith Robinson's article in last night's Toronto Telegram entitled "Gardiner's Barter Bargain".
Representatives of farm unions from five provinces are in Ottawa and I understand are trying to see as many members as they can to discuss a variety of problems. Yesterday they presented a brief to the government. One of the delegates, the vice-president of the farmers' union of Saskatchewan, saw me last night. I am sure that hon. members who do not want to accept our views on this problem would be well advised to see some of these delegates while they are in the city and get their opinions.
Grain *
The failure of the government to do something other than arrange for credit is actually going to cost the taxpayers a great deal of money directly. May I illustrate what I have in mind. Mr. Turnbull, vice-president of the farmers' union of Saskatchewan, has outlined what he is being forced to do with 10,000 bushels of wheat which he has on the ground. He is going to be obliged to go into hog production because there is a floor price under hogs, or so we are told.
One of his neighbours is putting up buildings in which to feed 500 hogs. That man has 15,000 bushels of barley on hand. As a result of our failure to recognize this problem there is going to be a tremendous increase in hog production and the taxpayers of Canada are going to have to subsidize pork production.
Mr. Turnbull mentioned that another farmer is acting on the advice of the Minister of Agriculture and is going to market his wheat through livestock. He is putting up pole shelters at a very low cost to house 200 head of cattle. No farmer in Ontario or Quebec can hope to compete with the sort of competition which is sure to develop.
The vice-president of the farmers' union is going to seed 200 acres with rapeseed this year because there is a guaranteed price. He knows that that will have an effect on butter producers. My colleague, the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson), acting last year on the suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture seeded 400 acres to rapeseed and had a production of 400,000 pounds. A process developed in Germany indicates that rapeseed will make a very palatable butter substitute.
I submit that it is most important that this bill to provide short-term credit to grain producers should not be read a second time. I think the Prime Minister should have an opportunity over the week end to consider the suggestions that I have made that these two members be given a chance to have a holiday. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the word "now" be left out, and the words "this day six months hence" be added at the end of the question.

Grain
There are a few things I wish to discuss on this second reading of Bill 82, an act to provide for assistance to farmers. The title of the bill is:
An act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
First of all I find that some of the subjects mentioned in the bill are a little difficult for me to follow. In the first place, I am of the opinion that the difficulty has not arisen particularly because of the farmer's inability to sell all of his grain. Certainly the difficulty has arisen because of the government's inability to sell the wheat of western Canada. It is not the farmer's job at all to sell this wheat. The government's policy should be so designed as to take care of the wheat of western Canada. The government has been solely responsible for the sale of wheat in this country. Therefore it is the government's responsibility now to see to it that the farmers are given assistance towards obtaining some cash in this time of emergency.
It is not my intention to establish need at this time, because I have already done that on another occasion during this debate and many members in the House of Commons have brought forth that very point. It has been well established by all soundthinking members that the western farmer is in need of assistance. I said that I thought the fact had been established by all soundthinking members in this house, but there are some members apparently who disagree with that point of view.
The thing that amazes me is that, despite the fact that almost every member, particularly from western Canada, has brought this to your attention, no Liberal members from Alberta have got up and spoken on Bill 82 which deals with this question. Why are they so profoundly silent? Certainly on other occasions they have made themselves heard. In view of the fact that the Liberal leader in the province of Alberta has come out and condemned this bill, I think it is about time some of the Liberal members from Alberta got up and made themselves known in this respect. Are they afraid of the whip that will be cracked over their heads if they get up and assert themselves on the side of the farmer? The people in Alberta who sent them down here expect them to get up and make a statement on this bill. It is vital to the welfare of the western agriculturists. 1 must say that I do give credit to some of the government backbenchers who have come to me personally and asked for my views on the situation of the farmers in western Canada. Those hon. members have an appreciation of the problems which exist in western Canada.
We cannot for one minute assume that farm conditions in other areas are similar to Saskatchewan. There are many factors which must be considered and a comparison of similar circumstances is most difficult. I suggest to members of the government that they would indeed be well advised to invite the western farm organizations-I am thinking of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the interprovincial farm union council and other prairie pools-to send representations down here to discuss the problems with them so that they may become acquainted with those problems.
The attitude of Saskatchewan Liberals is most unreliable and it is because of that unreliability that many Ontario and maritime members have spoken to me. I appreciate that fact and I appreciate the attitude they have adopted after I have discussed the problem with them. Many times they have said to me that they did not realize that things were that bad, that a farmer might have been able to sell only 300 bushels of grain when he had 5000 bushels in store on his farm.
I would point out that one of the inequalities which exists is in the distribution of box cars among the marketing points in western Canada. It is pointed out in the wheat review that there are many marketing points in Saskatchewan which are still on the initial unit basis. That means that the farmers at those points are allowed to deliver only 300 bushels of wheat. At the same time it is significant to note that a number of points are on the 3-bushel quota.
This indicates to me that the transport controller has not been paying close attention to the problem. There is a dispatch in today's Montreal Gazette which indicates that the transport controller has stated that the grain will be moved before the Canadian wheat board has made an estimate as to how much grain it will want moved. According to this article the controller stated that there is no shortage of box cars holding up prairie grain shipments.
If there is no shortage of box cars holding up prairie grain shipments then the Minister of Trade and Commerce should be severely criticized for allowing a situation to arise whereby there are 58 million bushels of storage space available in the terminals. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) has

denied any responsibility for filling up the terminals, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated that the moving of the wheat was not his responsibility. Those two ministers would be well advised to get a little closer together and give some thought to the position of the farmers of western Canada who are supposedly being served by the transport controller.
It is fairly obvious that members on the government side who are not conversant with this problem are creating a serious break in relations between western and eastern Canada. Their determination to prevent the introduction of any legislation which would prove to be of material assistance to western farmers is doing much to undermine the co-operation which must exist between all farmers of Canada if we are to achieve our fair share of the national income.
I do not think you will find many farmers on the western plains who will begrudge the freight rate assistance being provided for Ontario farmers, who will begrudge the assistance given to the maple sugar producers to purchase aluminum equipment, or who will begrudge other forms of direct and indirect assistance which have been given to the farmers in this area. I think also that eastern farmers generally have a great deal of sympathy for the western farmer.
I am making the statement now that if the government members continue to try to make a breach between the farmers of Canada, if they continue to be ignorant of the conditions which exist in western Canada, there can be only one answer or only one solution. I have heard this discussed many times during the last few months in Saskatchewan.
The people of western Canada are becoming fed up with the attitude of the government in denying them the South Saskatchewan dam and other things which would improve conditions in western Canada, so much so that they are considering marching on Ottawa. I must say that some of them are thinking in terms of secession.
I submit it is a pretty tragic indictment of the government of Canada when one section of the country realizes that it has been ignored, that it can no longer expect to get consideration from the government. It may be that if this Liberal government continues in power for too many years the only alternative will be for the western provinces to devise their own form of legislation so that they can be treated as they wish to be.
The challenge is out. I do not think any hon. member of this house will agree that the work done many years ago to bring about a national Canada should be so easily wrecked

by the failure of Liberal members from the prairies to present to their colleagues the conditions which exist in western Canada, present them with insistence in their party caucus and before this parliament of Canada. The challenge rests with them and I hope we will not be disappointed.

The farm union delegation is now in the city and what they have to say concerning the value of this piece of legislation with which we are dealing only confirms the convictions that have been held by a great many of us. It is a very sad commentary on conditions when a man has a piece of land which only two years ago was sold for $38,000. When he tried to get a mortgage on it for any amount, he was refused everywhere. I think that is a fairly common thing. I know areas in the west where 80 per cent of the farmers are now engaged in some other occupation in order to maintain a miserable standard of living.
When we have conditions such as these and at the same time find the granaries full of wheat, I think it is a very serious situation. I wish to refer now to a matter to which general reference has been made heretofore, and that is the general demand in the prairie provinces for cash advances on farm-stored wheat. The question that was passed as an order for return was as follows:
For a copy of all resolutions supporting the demand for cash advances on farm-stored wheat which have been received from western farm organizations and other public bodies, by the Prime Minister and any of the ministers of the government, or officials of the government, since the 15th day of August, 1955.
I have this return before me which tells the story. It indicates that more than 500
western farm organizations, municipalities and the like, have petitioned this government on behalf of what they demand, namely cash advances on farm-stored wheat.
One of the resolutions here is from Prince Albert and it is dated October 6, 1955, and signed by W. C. Bliss, Junior, subdistrict director of the Saskatchewan farmers' union, and represents the viewpoint of farmers generally in western Canada. After giving a general summary of the situation and the financial position in which the farmer finds himself, the resolution reads:
The most pressing problem is the shortage of cash, and we strongly urge the government to make cash advances on farm-stored grain in an amount not less than 85 per cent of the present initial payment.
It deals also with other matters and other demands of western farmers and ends up this way:
We urge that parliament be reconvened to take action . . . prompt and courageous action.
Now, this file has not shown all the returns because many of the resolutions were identical one with the other, but passed by more than 500 organizations throughout western Canada. It is for that reason I find it so difficult to understand why western Liberal members are adopting the attitude they are in this house on this matter. I have a tremendous regard for the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer). He has a scintillating wit and the power to make parliament really understand problems. I think he spoke with such power this morning when, in an interjection with an hon. member, he said in effect, in reply to the remark that he was stupid: "I am stupid because you cannot teach me anything". Well, in that statement I think the hon. gentleman seemed to be speaking generally, in reference to this particular matter, for those members of the Liberal party who represent constituencies in western Canada.

I simply say to my hon. friend I do not know what he is saying. I know it has nothing to do with the problem with which I am dealing, and as the cuckoo is in June, he is heard but not regarded.
I say to my hon. friend, in the last couple of days the farmers' union has made a submission and has set out in very careful detail the position of the gross and net farm income for all of Canada between 1951 and 1955, and also the gross and net income in the last several years. These statistics indicate the serious cash situation in which the farmer finds himself.
As far as Canada in general is concerned, starting with 1951, the gross and net income among farmers is set out as follows: In 1951 it went down by 10-72 per cent; in 1953, by 21-1 per cent; in 1954, by 48-2 per cent. The figures for 1955 will indicate a further reduction in net income. Net income, of course, is based on a relative comparison between gross income and the cost that the farmer has to incur in order to operate his farm. These costs are rising.
I now come to the gross and net farm income for the prairie provinces for the same period. In 1952 the net income was down by 3-13 per cent; in 1953, by 21-6 per cent; in 1954, by 66-64 per cent. The final 1955 figures are not yet available, but they will indicate a further decrease. A 66 per cent decrease in net farm income in a matter of three or four years is one which explains as clearly as possible the need of cash. If these figures were based upon the purchasing power of the dollar the condition of affairs would be even more serious than is apparent from the simple percentage statistics that I have placed before you, Mr. Speaker.
Farmers generally-and I say this cannot be contradicted; the return tells its story- want cash advances, and everything has been done to prevent their getting them. The minister has threatened; he has endeavoured to intimidate, all with a view to securing the passage of this bill, regardless of the demands of the western farmers. In one instance he has used a stick. I referred yesterday to a speech he made recently in which he enunciated that new principle of parliamentary freedom. On the occasion of the 20th anniversary celebration in honour of himself and of the Minister of Agriculture the stick was used, the toe-the-line philosophy. On the other hand, the carrot is held out as well, the promise to the farmers of western Canada that if this legislation is passed, then and then only will the government give consideration to making further advances or a distribution of moneys on account of 1954-55 pool.

That act was very similar, almost a counterpart except that the present legislation goes further and actually in effect places a yoke about the necks of western farmers. I quote from the 1951 legislation:
Where a person is convicted of an offence under this section there shall be imposed on him, in addition to any fine, a penalty equal to such amount of any guaranteed loan made to him in respect of which the offence was committed as has not been repaid by him, with interest thereon to the date of the conviction, and the penalty shall be paid to the bank-
If the farmer is proceeded against and fails to pay his fine, the alternative is jail. In addition to the fine there is also a penalty of the amount of the loan. I say that that type of thing is disgraceful legislation. It is actually providing for imprisonment for debt and it is adding to all the security of the Bank Act and the further security that is provided in that a farmer may not sell except when he makes payment and to the degree provided for the making of payment. If he commits an offence he immediately finds himself in the position of being subject, first to a penalty up to $500 and then in addition to be ordered to pay as a penalty the amount that he owes.
Grain
If he has made a misleading statement, if he does not get cash and is unable to pay the amount of the penalty, the amount of the loan, there is only one alternative open to him, prison. That is provided by the section in question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They have that in Saskatchewan if you do not pay.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am not going to disagree with my hon. friend. It just shows the degree to which this government is imitating the socialists in Saskatchewan with legislation such as this.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That was on the statute books before the C.C.F. were elected.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
This is a private argument between the C.C.F. and my hon. friend and I am simply an onlooker. I pass on to this legislation of 1951. In 1951 conditions were such that legislation similar to the present act was placed upon the statute books. We said that insufficient had been voted-$20 million was the amount-and ever since the right hon. gentleman has pointed out to us that the legislation was not used. He asked me to quote, and I shall quote what he had to say on November 18, 1953, as reported on page 128 of Hansard. At that time he was giving the reasons why advances on the farm, as be called them, were not necessary. I quote:
It will be understood, then, why the government considers that the need for farm advances has not been proven.
The government also had before it the results of the legislation approved by parliament In 1951 for advances to producers of grain on farms. Hon. members will recall the circumstances of that year. A very large crop had been grown but a great deal of it was tough and damp and a very large area was under snow and could not then be harvested. Faced with this situation, which was certainly very much grimmer than now prevails, the government introduced a bill to provide shortterm advances to farmers. The banks were to be guaranteed against losses on loan advances up to $20 million on both grain in storage and grain in the fields.
After a few pleasantries directed at myself-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Better read it all, do not skip anything.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman had this to say:
I regret to say, however, that even though advances under this 1951 legislation were very limited and one might have thought that the risk was negligible, over $40,000 is still outstanding and the Department of Finance has paid losses to the banks in excess of $11,000. These results must cause anyone to pause who advocates that the wheat board or the treasury should become involved in a widespread system of advances on farm-held grain.

Grain
He said the legislation did not work, that it was worthless, and then in order to show how worthless it was he duplicates it in 1956 and asks the farmers to accept that which he said was not successful in 1951. Is it any wonder that in 1951 the farmers did not accept that kind of legislation? They were not looking for passports to jail, they were looking for advances which would make available to them the necessary money to pay their current expenses.
What happened-I say this with great respect-to the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) a few days ago simply summarized the attitude of western farmers everywhere. As a matter of fact, if I might be allowed to paraphrase-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Something more.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend will understand this because he was an American until recent years. Paraphrasing Emerson I would say: Here once the embattled farmers stood and fired their shots heard around the west. That represents the attitude of western farmers everywhere. They are demanding that cash advances be provided. The record before us indicates the extent of that demand.
If the legislation did not work in 1951 why embalm it in another piece of legislation which is almost a photographic copy except for the amount which the banks may lend and also the extension of the penalties provided in 1951. The reason given by the minister in 1953 was that this kind of thing could not be done because the farmers were dishonest, because they were evading it, and because we have suffered loss. Ever since 1951 whenever any member of the opposition has suggested that something should be done to assist the farmers by cash advances on farm-stored grain the minister has bravely stood his ground and pointed out that the 1951 experiment was unsuccessful, that it did not work, that only a very small percentage of the total amount guaranteed was taken over by the farmers.
That is the reason for the small amount. What is the percentage? I understand it is about 4 per cent of the farmers. Four per cent have taken advantage of this, and that is all. They have been forced into that position against their own wishes and desires, against the resolutions which they themselves joined in having passed.
That is the reason why we take the stand that we do, and it has been a consistent stand. Last September when the matter was first mentioned, with the approval and consent of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) I said that we believed in cash advances and that parliament should be called

together. When the Leader of the Opposition was in western Canada in October and November and saw the situation he reiterated over and over again the need for action along this line being taken. But parliament was not called. If parliament had been called, the whole matter could have been discussed. Instead of that, the back-door method of cabinet decree was used and we are asked in parliament to rubber-stamp what the government did when it acted in derogation to everything the western farmer has demanded.
I was surprised this morning to hear the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking) make a statement which in some ways seems to epitomize the viewpoint of some of my hon. friends opposite. Referring to the western farmers, he said this: "Your farmer will certainly do some work for a change."
That was a statement that ought not to have been made. I would like to see some of the Liberal members from Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta stand up and repudiate that-unless my hon. friend has indeed become the voice of the members of the province of Ontario supporting the government. That was a very serious statement. We are not asking for any handouts. The government is the only market, through the wheat board. The farmer is entitled to what he has earned. Being in that position, he resents having to pay interest on the work he has done. We took that stand first in September, then when our leader visited western Canada, then again in the initial speech made in this House of Commons this session by the hon. gentleman, and also during the month of December when we said, as far as the resolution stage was concerned, "We shall accept this, because apparently something is going to be done."
I say, with all respect to the Department of National Revenue, which seems to have a monopoly of this sort of thing, that what is produced is almost a photostatic copy of a bill that did not work then. We were defeated when we asked that it be submitted to the agriculture committee. What we are trying to do is to secure through parliament by parliamentary means what the western farmer is asking for and what he has demanded over and over again. It may be that in the stand we take, because of the overwhelming government majority, this legislation will be pushed through. If it is, my answer to those who push it through is that if the 1951 legislation does not work, this legislation cannot work either. The experience of the past few months and the degree to which it has not been made use of indicates that it does not meet the situation.

indeed, this problem is one that recurs from year to year. Not every year, but from time to time, it has recurred since 1952. In November 1953 the Leader of the Opposition, then speaking as I say he was speaking, for those in western Canada who had been asking for this kind of thing, demanded that legislation providing for cash advances should indeed be brought into effect. When finally the bill came up for second reading, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) showed the attitude of this party in the amendment he tried to move, but it was ruled out of order. That amendment-and I am now paraphrasing-provided that the bill be not now read the second time but that there be substituted therefor legislation to provide for cash payments on farm-stored grain. In other words, cash advances are what we in this party have demanded over and over again. The support we have given to them is indicated by what I mentioned a moment ago-our support of similar legislation in 1953 and since.
Apparently even among members of the government there was not very much certainty as to what they were going to do. You will remember when Mr. McDonald, the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan, came here-I think it was in October-and said something had to be done. He said, "I can't tell you what it is." It is like the old Indian medicine, Kickapoo juice; it would cure anything, but they never told you the contents. He returned and said, "I have found it; I have got it." Then it was rumoured that the plan was indeed guaranteed bank loans. On October 24, 1955, the Minister of Agriculture, speaking in Winnipeg, said that while there were complaints, including a complaint from the Manitoba government, these complaints were based on a belief that the federal government had chosen bank loans rather than advances. He said, in effect, "Don't believe it." There was the criticism of the Manitoba government and its representative. There has been the criticism of the leader of the Liberal party in Alberta, who knows what the people think.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

question of privilege. It is bad enough to misquote a member of this house, but I think to misquote someone outside the house, who is not here to defend himself, is not right.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is his privilege, is it?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am afraid what the minister has raised is not a true question of privilege in the House of Commons.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend does no better at interpreting the feelings of the western farmers than he does at interpreting
Grain
what Mr. Prowse said the other day on television, then I am very sorry for the people of Alberta. Everywhere throughout the western provinces the farmers are asking that we take action in this parliament to meet the situation.
I make this last appeal, that the government reconsider the matter now. I know that in recent weeks of this session, this government has scintillated in confusion, but I hope that out of the confusion of jarring statements made by various ministers since October last will come at last a realization that what the western farmer wants is cash advances. If even now they will withdraw this legislation and bring in what the farmer wants, it would be assured of immediate passage in this house.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not had a great deal to say on this matter in the past week or so, because I have felt that there were many others who wished to speak and that they should be accorded every opportunity of doing so. In this group we are fortunate in having with us most of the practising farmers on this side of the house, and I have been very happy indeed that, while I represent a constituency that is primarily interested in this problem, we have men who are actually engaged in production-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should correct that and say "western farmers". I have risen this afternoon to make one or two observations I have wanted to make for some time. I want to say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that the position in which western farmers have been placed by this situation is deeply resented by them. I informed the minister of a constituent of mine who for two reasons, one because he needed the storage space and the other because he needed cash, was actually selling 1954 feed wheat to the stockyards in Saskatoon for a cent a pound and paying 20 cents a bushel for hauling it. In other words, he was getting a net of 40 cents a bushel at Rosetown, Saskatchewan, for that wheat. When you examine the value of the dollar today compared with what it was in the 1930's, about which we have so often talked in this house, that means that in pre-war currency he was getting about 19 cents a bushel or about the lowest price that farmers in that area got for their wheat at the elevator in the very depths of the depression.
I am not going very fully into the legislation before us this afternoon because it has been gone into by so many. It is unsatisfactory legislation. It is legislation which we

Grain
saw introduced in 1951 and which we opposed at that time by an amendment to the resolution urging the government at that time to adopt a policy of cash advances. That has been our plea in the house ever since 1951. I am going to say to the minister that I am not in agreement with those who say that because we have a surplus of wheat at the moment on the western prairies our farmers should be told to cut down their production of wheat next year. I am not sure when that wheat will be needed in view of the reports coming to us from Europe at the present time that hundreds of thousands, yes, millions of acres of winter wheat have been destroyed by the great frost in Europe. Next year, or the year after this, wheat may be a very valuable asset to Canada and to the world.
I am never one of those who believe in restricting production to meet a situation of this sort, but I am saying that this valuable reserve, this valuable asset to Canada and to the world should not be carried by the farmers who produced it but that the people who should carry the burden are the people of this dominion. Of course it can be done in two ways, by making cash advances repayable when the wheat is marketed on a quota basis and then the surplus stored and storage paid to the farmers who have their wheat properly stored to meet the future needs of people here and across the world.
As was said this morning, because of the inability of the farmer to market his grain and his inability to get cash advances which would enable him to build more adequate and safe storage space, there has been a serious deterioration of wheat on the western prairies which we as a nation and the world may regret in the days to come. I have never had very much faith in the government's protestations about the wheat board. I am very glad that recently in the debate we have not heard it said that those of us on this side of the house are weakening or undermining the wheat board. That can be demonstrated to be quite untrue. As a matter of fact the records clearly prove on which side of the house the people sit who through the years have been supporters of the orderly system of marketing.
I regret that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is not in his seat this afternoon. Last night he accused me again of having misrepresented him on many occasions over recent years. I have no recollection of having done so except in so far as I said a few days ago that I had been misinformed and that I had misquoted the Minister of Agriculture. I admitted that and put the record straight. But the Minister of

Agriculture is constantly saying that he has been misrepresented either in the press or in this house. He said it last night when it so happened that I had the Hansard on my desk from which I am going to quote in a moment.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) was referring to a statement made in the house by the Minister of Agriculture on April 5, 1939, and the minister disputed the accuracy of the statement of the hon. member for Mackenzie. I happened to have the Hansard with the verbatim report of what the Minister of Agriculture said. It is true that speaking from memory the hon. member for Mackenzie left out the reference to 20 bushels to the acre, but otherwise the statement was correct in every particular.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Was not the 20
bushels to the acre the essential part of the statement?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I would not say that was the essential part of the statement. If the minister thinks so I will not argue that point, but in any event the matter was cleared up immediately. The accurate statement was placed on the record last night from Hansard of that date. Last night the hon. member for Mackenzie said, as found at page 1276 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, when the matter comes up again I will have the reference in Hansard and I will be very glad to place it on the record.
Then I said, "Here you are." Then the Minister of Agriculture said:
The hon. gentleman who has misrepresented it for all these years is now handing it to you.
I have not misrepresented it. I have not referred to it for some years now but whenever I did I used to carry with me a copy of the Hansard for April 5, 1939, and read what the minister had said from the record.
I went further and read more than what was read last night although I do not think it made a material difference to the argument in question that, if we raised 20 bushels or more to the acre, wheat could be produced at 30 to 40 cents a bushel in western Canada. But the other day I was speaking in the house and I said this in this same debate-I am not quoting from a previous debate but the same debate-as found at page 843 of Hansard of February 3:
... I remember perfectly well the Minister of Agriculture rising on occasion after occasion in the house and defending the grain exchange method of marketing.
The minister said, "Oh, no." Then I said:
Hon. members who were in the house at the time, and I am sorry to say there are only a very few of us left, can remember it as vividly as I can.

Then the minister said:
... My hon. friend should not quote unless he has Hansard here to prove it.
One reason I am speaking this afternoon is that I have Hansard here to prove it. In the same debate the minister said that he had not supported the competitive system of marketing, which is the grain exchange method of marketing, since he had been in the house. Well, here is the record. Speaking in the debate on April 5, 1939, he referred to a speech of the late Hon. J. L. Ralston, to which I had referred, and said, as found at page 2612 of Hansard of that date:
Hon. J. L. Ralston, speaking in 1935 for the Liberal party, then the official opposition, on the grain bill of that year, which later became the wheat bill, and replying to Mr. Bennett, said, as reported at page 3581 of Hansard:
"I do not believe that the people of the Dominion of Canada are favourable to a compulsory wheat board, to a board the constitution of which will mean that every wheat grower, every elevator man and everybody engaged in the wheat business must deal with the government agency and no one else. This matter of policy has been discussed before not only in this house but throughout the country. The government has carried on with a voluntary system for five years as Mr. McFarland and the Canadian Co-Operative Wheat Producers Limited have been nothing more or less than a board conducting voluntary market operations. A man was entitled to sell or not sell to Mr. McFarland as he saw fit. I submit that so far as the western wheat grower is concerned that the voluntary system should be continued until there has been more opportunity to consider the matter. I do not believe the compulsory feature of this bill will meet with approval, either in the west, in the east or in this house."
That is the end of the quotation. Then the minister added these words:
There you have the issue clearly drawn between the two parties at that time-
I will refer to those words in a moment. -in the house: One was for compulsion: the other-
The Liberal party.
-was for a continuance of the voluntary system.
Those were the words of the minister in this house on April 5, 1939. Then he went on to discuss the undertakings that Mr. Bennett had given at the time the wheat board was under discussion and he said this:
When these undertakings were given, indicating that the legislation was to deal with a temporary condition, that it was not a permanent policy, and that even while it was in force it was subject to the control of the government of the day, it passed the house unanimously.
I place this record on Hansard in order that the position may be quite clear in any discussion which may take place in regard to the actions of the government from that day to this, whether under the previous prime minister or the present Prime Minister.
Then my hon. friend the minister went [DOT]on to describe some of the operations of
Grain
the wheat board under Mr. McFarland and subsequently, at page 2615 of Hansard of 1939, having clearly outlined all this, he summarises what we took to be his own opinion in the matter. He says:
I have come to the conclusion that to ignore the so-called law of supply and demand, as Mr. Bennett said his government intended to do when they brought in the first bill in 1935, will eventually wreck any system that can be devised, by loading the system with an enormous surplus or by giving it an enormous deficit.
There we have the record indicating quite clearly that the statement which I made- and which the minister denied-was perfectly correct in every particular. I had, of course, quoted a former minister of agriculture, the late Hon. W. R. Motherwell, to the effect that he had been deceived, that when he wished to market his grain through his own local elevator through the wheat board, he was unable to do so in 1938.

speechtext: As a matter of fact, I thought he would be here.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member picks his days.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
No; I do not pick days. If the minister really wants to know the truth, I may tell him that I did not speak yesterday because I was not well. That was the only reason. Perhaps I should not be speaking this afternoon. But I want to say that what I have tried to do is correct a statement which the minister made in reply to a statement that I had made that afternoon.
I hear from a good many of the wheat producers in western Canada. My constituency is wholly a wheat-producing constituency. I was over the whole of it last autumn from one end to the other. My constituents at various points-and all of them are wheat farmers-expressed deep resentment at the

Grain
proposal once again to introduce this bank loan plan which-as the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said in the speech he has just made-was proved to be a failure in 1953. We knew that it would be not only unpopular but mainly useless in 1951 when we moved the amendment to which I have referred calling for advances. We are therefore opposing this legislation because we disbelieve in it, because we think it is inadequate and because we think it is resented by the people who sent us here, and we are saying so. Not only are we saying so but at every opportunity we are going to vote against it.
I know we were the only party in the house which voted against it at the resolution stage. We voted against it then because we hoped that if the house showed its disapproval of this legislation at the resolution stage, a bill such as the one we have before us might not be introduced but rather that the government might reconsider its proposals and introduce another bill designed to meet the needs of the western wheat growers. I think that is what they hoped for as well. The government have not seen fit to do so. They have adopted this policy and they are going to put it through, I have no doubt. But they will put it through over our opposition.
Let it not be said that the opposition that has been indicated in this house to this measure is in any way fomented by those who are opposed to the wheat board. That was said on occasion but I am glad to say it has not been said just lately. Let that not be said. The Winnipeg Free Press, the newspaper which has been said to be opposed to the board, was opposed to the board, I know, when the board was originally set up and for some years afterwards. But as I read the Free Press today, even it accepts the situation as an accomplished fact, realizing that the producers want such a method of marketing and realizing perhaps that with an international wheat agreement-which I may say I hope will be consummated-this is the only way in which wheat can be marketed successfully under agreements and on the markets of the world. Hence today I believe there is unanimity in Canada-except for a minority who would like to restore the entire grain business to the grain exchange-in support of the wheat board method of marketing. We therefore do not need to argue that point.
I am going to say this to my hon. friends of the Liberal party. While I have said-and it is my belief-that they were opposed to this method of marketing for a long time, and that they wanted to do all they could to keep the
[Mr. Coldwell.l
voluntary system or, as they call it, the competitive system, because of the experience of the government during the war years and subsequently I believe they, like the rest of us, now believe that the wheat board is here to stay and that it is the best method of marketing.
But that does not mean that, under circumstances such as those which now exist, our farmers are able to market enough grain to pay their expenses and their taxes; and those taxes are an extremely serious consideration in all the three western provinces where wheat is grown in large quantities. The municipalities in Manitoba, in Saskatchewan and in Alberta are all finding it difficult to maintain their essential services and their school systems. These bank loans will not suffice. If a man can get a bank loan under this legislation, he can get a bank loan anyway. If he is marketing some of his wheat, the bank loan he will get is so small that it will make little difference to him and it will not enable him to pay his taxes or to prepare his machinery for seeding in the springtime. So it is that we are opposing this legislation because we should like to have seen something different. Today, of course, I suppose it does not matter, from the point of view of the western farmers, whether or not this legislation is supported by the opposition members. Loans have been made and the guarantee was given by the Minister of Defence Production-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris).

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, the guarantee was given by the Minister of Finance to the banks, and I have no doubt that guarantee will be carried out. I want to say this to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), who is also not in his seat: When this was contemplated the proper thing to have done was to have called parliament together to have this legislation, if this was to be the legislation, passed by the house.
I think the pledging of money on behalf of Canada is not a matter that can be done by order in council. If there is one traditional right we have in this House of Commons, it is the control over expenditure. It may be a very shadowy thing in a house where the government has the huge majority it has in this parliament, but the real function of this house it not to initiate legislation, which is the business of the government, but to control expenditures. This might have been a very heavy expenditure. I do not know what amounts are out at the moment but I imagine they are relatively small and yet, in many

people's eyes, probably quite substantial. This has been done without the consent of this parliament.
Parliament should have been called together when the situation was realized last September, and provision made, not for bank loans or loans upon which the farmers would have to pay 5 per cent interest on what has been described in this house as their own earnings. At the same time we were told that a powerful company, controlled in almost every particular in the United States, would have very great advances, not in the form of actual cash but in the form of a great national project which I think should not be alienated, at 3-5 per cent interest. The contrast is striking, Mr. Speaker. So I am rising this afternoon to support the amendment we have moved, just as I rose to support the other amendment we moved, to give this the six months' hoist.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
We have listened to this debate for some time, Mr. Speaker, and I was going to say mostly but I will say nearly all the speeches from the opposition were irrelevant or repe-titous. I think, therefore, we on this side of the house have good reason for not intervening in the debate to prolong it uselessly. But having just listened to the speech by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) and the speech by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) I think that one or two remarks would be in order at this time.
In my opinion the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar put his finger on the crux of the problem when he said he is of the opinion that the surplus wheat we have in the west at this time is a great national asset. In saying that, he is repeating what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has already said, that it is no calamity to have a great wheat surplus because at this time they have bad weather conditions in Europe which may lead to a bad crop and we will undoubtedly sell our wheat crop eventually.

speechtext: May I say-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
What impressed me most in what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, if the hon. member will allow me to continue, was that he thought the people of Canada should pay for the carrying of this surplus wheat; that is the crux of the problem. We on this side think that money should be advanced to the farmers but that they should pay interest on it. The people on the other side think that money should be advanced to the farmers without interest. Who is going to pay the interest? Evidently it is the people of Canada. Is it fair that the people of
Grain
Canada should be called upon to pay interest for the farmers in the west? Why should I not say, as the member for the Madeleine islands, that the people of Canada should pay interest to the fishermen on their fish products that have been canned but not sold or that have been frozen and not sold. There are many other instances. You could go to the coal mines or anything that is produced in the country.
You could say, why should the people of Canada not make advances on all of these things that are produced? Why should they pay interest on such money? I think what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has stated illustrates how weak is the position of the opposition and how strong is the position of the government. He has put his finger right on it. Why should the people of Canada pay that interest for the western farmers if they do not pay interest for all the other producers of this country?
Now, I want to mention what the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said. I am sorry he has left the house. He has a reputation, which I am sure is well deserved, of being a distinguished lawyer. He has made a statement that I think is a legal heresy. His statement was more or less along the same line as that of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. He says the farmers have produced this wheat, and therefore they should be paid for it and they should not have to pay interest on the money they get for it, whether or not the wheat is sold. There again, you cannot support a statement like that if you have a legal brain and if you know what the law is all about. Why should a person be paid for something he has produced before that thing has been sold? Why should he get that money without having to pay interest on it? I think perhaps all the western farmers can expect us to do for them is just what we are doing, to facilitate their getting bank loans on which they pay interest. It is only the normal thing. Why should they get money on their products, without paying interest, without having sold their products?
I think we are doing the right thing for the farmers. I am sure the farmers in the west are just as good citizens as any of us are. I am sure they are pleased with the legislation we are passing for them, which is privileged legislation, but I do not begrudge it. I am sure they realize they are getting a privilege through this legislation. I am sure the members of the opposition, and particularly the members of the C.C.F. group who have carried on a filibuster against this legislation, have not gained one vote but on the contrary have lost votes in the western part of the country.
