speechtext:
I wish to say a few words on Bill No. 82, Mr. Speaker. A number of us in this group at the resolution stage criticized the government's proposal at some length. On the other hand, it was a resolution to introduce a bill and we did not vote against the resolution because we wanted to see just what was going to be in the bill. We wanted to be in a position to accept or reject the bill on its merits. After we read the bill, there was no doubt in our minds that the bill should be rejected. Therefore, when the C.C.F. moved an amendment to report the subject matter of this bill to the committee on agriculture, we supported it.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) suggested that such action would kill the bill. However, I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) showed quite clearly that that would not necessarily be the result, but that the subject matter could be sent to the committee on agriculture, and if the committee saw fit it could recommend to the house that the bill be again presented. Then, the bill could be put through the house if the house saw fit. Therefore the argument of the minister was not a very sound one.
However, I did present an alternative to the government. I suggested that after second reading the bill itself should be sent to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. There was nothing unique about the proposal. We do it every year. At the time I was somewhat disappointed, but I will not say surprised, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) rejected the suggestion and said the government was not prepared to send the bill to the committee. I think it is a pity. It is quite an important measure. I should like to see a bill of this kind given far more consideration than it is going to get, and perhaps be extended into something of a permanent character, useful in the future instead of just for the moment. If this bill had been sent to the agriculture committee and we had called representatives from various farm organizations, then they could have given their views on the bill itself.
I do not know whether the government actually consulted any of the officials of the main farm organizations on the drafting of this bill. I doubt very much whether they did because I was speaking to one of the officials of one of the main farm organizations just two days ago, and I asked him what he thought of the bill. He said: "I have never seen it". He has not the slightest idea what is in the bill. He could not say whether he was in favour of it or not until he had seen it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question? Is it customary to issue copies of bills before they are introduced in the house?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No; but in a matter of this kind, in view of the fact that the minister had been out west and as a result of that visit came to the conclusion that loans should be made, it would have been a wise act on his part to call representatives of the unions down to Ottawa and discuss with them just what they thought should be in the legislation. In so far as agriculture is concerned- I may be wrong in this-I have a very strong feeling that the government acted differently in regard to the banks. I am not suggesting that the government issued the bill to the banks before it was introduced, although that may be possible, but I am pretty sure they consulted closely with the banks relative to various sections of the bill. If banks are to be consulted in that way regarding matters in the bill relating to them, surely it would have been a matter of courtesy, if nothing else, to give the same privilege to farm organizations. The minister could have very well discussed those sections that he intended to put into the bill relating to farmers because there are some features in the bill that I am satisfied the farmers will bitterly resent when they learn about them. At the present time they do not know about them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that responsible farm leaders well known to my hon. friend suggested that we use the form of legislation of 1951.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Well, the situation in 1951 was very different from this one. What did you have then? You had your wheat unthreshed under the snow on the prairies. There was quite a question whether or not that wheat would ever be harvested at all. Undoubtedly, a great deal of risk was involved. What is the situation today? The grain is in the bins and the loans have been made on only a percentage of the grain, on only 50 per cent, I would imagine.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for a small farmer it could be 100 per cent.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Well

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: This bill is meant to help the small farmer.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Only half of each delivery is to be paid to the banks. Therefore, it must be 50 per cent. Otherwise, what has happened to the other 50 per cent? It is not 100 per cent; it is 50 per cent. Therefore, I say it is only a percentage of the wheat against which the loans are to be made; just

Grain
half the wheat. If a farmer should have
10.000	bushels and loans are made against only 5,000 bushels, the most he could get would be $5,000, but actually the maximum loan is only $1,500, therefore a man would need at least 3,000 bushels of wheat to get a $1,500 loan.
As I say, there are a number of features of this legislation which are of a very questionable character. When the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) spoke the other night-I am going to use his own words, especially since he is not in his seat- he said this, as reported at page 1218 of Hansard:
By suggesting that this bill should be sent to the committee on agriculture and colonization they are in tact saying that the western farmers are in no hurry for cash advances of any kind and can afford to wait for months and months.
By "they" he meant the members of the opposition.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Is that not right?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
That is where you are absolutely wrong. They do not have to wait for months. Loans are already being made. Over
8.000	farmers have had loans up to the end of December, according to the figures given by the minister. I think $7 million has already been lent.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You are learning something.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The average loan is around $800. There is no question of the farmers having to wait. It makes very little difference whether this legislation goes through today or a month hence. Loans have been made in a large number of cases and I suppose they will continue to be made.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member said they were not getting them.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: If the hon. member would just listen he would not make an unwise statement like that. Let me finish what I have to say on this point. Loans have been made, 8,000 of them. I will guarantee that the majority of those loans would have been made whether this legislation had gone through or not. If this legislation were withdrawn tomorrow the banks would continue to lend in the same way as they have lent in the past. Why have the farmers hung back? For the simple reason that they do not like going into debt when they have wheat in the bin and they want to sell it. They want to sell wheat, not borrow money on it. Why should they borrow money on that wheat in order to pay bills? That is what most are doing.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Will the hon. member permit a question? Why should farmers get cash
advances on their wheat without paying interest on it any more than any other primary producer in Canada?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Do you pay interest on the butter floor price?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Let me finish this other point. The point I was making is that the farmers are getting the loans, and will continue to get the loans even though this legislation is not passed.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They are paying interest.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, of course. That is the reason. The reason they have not asked for loans is that they do not want to pay interest. They are hoping to be able to sell the wheat. That is the reply to the hon. member who just rose to his feet. The reason the farmers should not have to pay interest is this. The government is in control of the marketing of wheat and of transportation. Last year sales broke down. They could not get orders. This year they could get orders but they could not get box cars. It is transportation that has broken down. The government is in full charge of that policy. The farmers have a right to expect the government to at least pay them the price of the normal delivery for wheat on the farm. That is all they are asking for, the normal delivery of wheat. Why should they pay interest on that?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They have already sold more than an average crop.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
That shows just how little the hon. member knows. The minister himself said that some points have a one-bushel quota. Is that a normal crop? Some points have a 2-bushel quota, and some have a 3-bushel quota. Does the hon. member call that an average crop? It might be in his part of the country, but if so, he must live on a stone pile. That is certainly not the situation in western Canada where the average yield even in an average year was around 17 bushels. In the past five years the average yield has been considerably in excess of that amount.
While I say there is a 1-bushel quota at some points, there are many farmers at those points who have not been able to deliver one bushel on the 1-bushel quota. Most points have been able to deliver the initial amount of 300 bushels, but there are many farmers who have not been able to deliver one bushel on the 1-bushel quota. It is not very pleasant for those farmers when they see a point 30 miles away where the farmers can sell three bushels to the acre and they are unable to sell one. As a result of that situation they

Grain
have bills in town at the different stores unpaid. They would like to pay them. They are not paying any interest on those bills. Can you blame them for not going to borrow money and pay interest on it in order to pay another bill upon which they are not paying any interest? It would not be very good business; it might be good ethics. That is why many farmers are taking loans today to pay bills on which they do not have to pay any interest. They are doing that because they like to pay their debts. They would rather pay interest on the debt to the hanks than continue to allow the bill to run in the store, because they realize it is a hardship on the storekeeper. I would say that is true of 95 per cent of the cases. It just goes to prove that the farmers of the west, as a rule, are honest men and like to pay their debts. But they think there should be a limit to the extent to which they should be plunged steadily further and further into debt. They have the right to expect that they should be able to deliver a normal delivery. All that the farmers in the constituency that I represent ask for is for the government to make an advance up to 50 per cent of the normal delivery. By advance in that case they meant payment on the wheat and not a loan. They rejected the idea of a loan. They suggested that the normal delivery should be on the basis of 8 bushels to the acre because they were afraid that if it stated merely the normal delivery the government might take only 2 or 3 bushels to the acre. That is the stand they have taken to date. I have absolutely no hesitation in saying that if they read this bill they will reject it.
The farmers did not tell me that. As a matter of fact when matters of this kind come before a convention in my constituency and I try to get the farmers to give me a directive as to whether I should vote for or against something, they have always insisted that I use my best judgment. They say, "You are on the spot; you know the facts; therefore we are going to leave it to your discretion to decide whether you vote for or against the measure." I am using my discretion at the present time in rejecting this bill. The title of the bill reads:
An act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
I suppose that could be said to be the purpose of the bill. I would appreciate the minister correcting me if I am wrong, but I gathered from what he said that the purpose of the bill is to make loans available to the weaker farmer, the small farmer, the new farmer or the farmer who is financially embarrassed. I take it that is the main purpose

of the bill, that is the class he has in view. I think he will agree that this is a fair interpretation of his attitude. I do not wish to misinterpret him and it would take too long to find his actual statement by going through all the pages of Hansard. I take it that this is the general purpose.
Therefore the minister will agree that if that is the purpose it is most important that this bill should carry out that purpose. I claim that the bill does not carry out that purpose. As a matter of fact, I claim that many farmers who might borrow under this bill will be worse off than farmers who borrow from other sources. I will give the reason why I say I think it will actually worsen their position. My contention is that the contents of this bill violate the purposes of the bill. We have heard it said that some members are dirt farmers, that some have had no farming experience. Speaking personally, I think I am in as good a position as anyone to speak on this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You do not need the bill then.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, I do not need the bill. I am not supporting or rejecting this bill on the basis of what I need, I am supporting or rejecting it on the basis of what I feel the people in the area I represent need. I have farmed for some 40 years. Let me state frankly that 75 per cent of that time I was short of capital. I have had lots of experience in borrowing from banks, so I know something about this situation. It is true that for the last 25 per cent of the time I probably did not need to, but for the first 75 per cent I did.
I homesteaded in the west in 1909. I did not have any capital, I did not have any money at all. I used to work in railway construction camps for a few months in the summer in order to get enough money to run my farm.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You have done pretty well in this country under the Liberals.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I have done fairly well in spite of the Liberals, you might say.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: There are a lot of people in the same boat from the sound of it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
By 1914 I had just started to get on my feet, and then I was overseas for five years. When I came back I had to start all over again. Everything I had was worn out, my machinery was all worn out and the price of everything was sky high. I settled under the Soldier Settlement Act which was a pretty tough act, quite different from the present Veterans' Land Act. Within a few

years the value of my chattels had fallen to about half their original value. It was about 1929 before I again started to get on my feet.
In 1929 I was still farming with horses. I realized then, as did most farmers, that if I was going to make any real progress I would have to have a mechanized farm. I went to the bank and asked for a loan in order to buy a tractor. I was quite interested in the attitude taken by the bank manager. He had my financial statement and he told me I was in excellent shape, that in a short time I would be sitting on top of the world, but he then went on to give me some sound advice. He told me not to borrow any money with which to buy a tractor because within a short period of time we would be going into a depression.
That was in 1929. I have always wondered why a bank manager was able to tell me in 1929-it was not being publicized in the press -that we were going into a depression when credit would be restricted and therefore it would be unwise for me to buy a tractor. I continued along with my horses. Just two years later I went to the bank again, but I could not borrow a cent although my physical assets were exactly the same or a little bit better than in 1929. In 1929 I could have borrowed enough on my personal note to buy a tractor, but in 1931 I could not borrow a cent.
I might mention that they had changed the bank manager in the meantime. Any time they bring in a new policy of restricting loans they seem to change their managers, because it might embarrass a bank manager to refuse a loan to an old friend. I thought it very strange that with no change in physical assets I could not borrow any money.
We all remember the depression, and I am not going to deal with it. We got through it. I did not go under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act because I did not like it, just as I do not like this bill. There were too many restrictions in it. However, we farmers got through the depression and then came some good times. I admit quite frankly that we have had some good times.
There are many farmers who realized that in order to produce efficiently they had to have an efficient unit. Professor Hope has defined an efficient unit as two sections of moderate land or one section of heavy land. The area which I represent is a good one, and many farmers thought it advisable to expand their land holdings and borrowed money with which to buy land. They borrowed money to buy farm machinery under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
Those are the farmers who are in so much difficulty today. They are not new farmers,
Grain
they are not young farmers, they are not small farmers; they are fairly large farmers. They have been farming quite a long time and have lots of experience. But they have incurred heavy liabilities which normally would be met from their sales of wheat. These are the farmers who are facing a great deal of difficulty.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Do you think our eastern farmers should supply the money for the loans?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Get up and make your own speech.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am. It is short and to the point, and I am not delaying the debate.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
You want to know whether I think the eastern farmer should be prepared to pay income tax for the purpose of helping to pay interest or to make loans available without interest? There need not be any interest involved, because the government could make advances to the farmers and get the money from its own institution, the Bank of Canada, without borrowing from the chartered banks. But it goes far beyond that. Even if it was costing some money I say that the western farmers are entitled to it because during the latter part of the war they subsidized the consumers of Canada to the tune of around $136 million. The same thing applies to other products of the farm.
Therefore a suggestion like that does not embarrass me at all. The hon. member talks about income tax. Let me remind him that the majority of the income taxes paid by farmers is paid by farmers in the west and not by farmers in the east. I suggest it would be a good idea if the Minister of National Revenue sent as many inspectors into that part of the country as to the west; then they would collect a little more money. The only reason they collect more income tax in the west is the fact that wheat is one of the main products and it is very easy for the Department of National Revenue to check on the farmers' incomes. In the east, where the farmers peddle their products in the local markets, there is no check at all, and I think many of them get away with murder.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Is that the only reason your farmers are honest?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Sell your gas.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sorry the minister went away, though the parliamentary assistant is here, because I do not like to say anything specifically referring to the minister when he is out. I was just going to say that I have been puzzled at times' during this debate over the fact that the minister seems to display

Grain
quite an ignorance of the true situation in regard to agriculture. However, that is perhaps only natural, because he is not a farmer and the problems are quite complex.
I believe he thinks he is stating the facts when he makes certain statements, but when I spoke the last time he made two or three interjections, and I was somewhat amazed at the questions he asked. I should have thought he must have known at that time that his questions did not really make sense, as for instance when he suggested that no large farmer had trouble getting money from the banks.
I have just explained why so many farmers are having trouble. It is because many of the big farmers have borrowed to expand their capital in the form of machinery, and have borrowed to expand their land holdings. They are large farmers, but they are heavily in debt. They may have 20,000 or 30,000 bushels of wheat on the farm but cannot sell it. If they could sell their wheat they would be able to meet their obligations. They cannot borrow money from the bank because they have gone as far as they can go in that direction. They are not interested in legislation like this. They are interested in being able to sell their wheat.
Right through this debate the minister has shown that he does not understand the situation as between the smaller farmer and the larger farmer. He jumped to the conclusion that the large farmer must be considerably better off than a small farmer. I agree that the size of the farm is a great factor, but there is another factor even greater, and that is the quality of the soil. You could have a three-section unit of marginal land which would not be nearly as good as a one-section unit in, for instance, gumbo land.
The constituency I represent is remarkable for the different types of soil it contains. On the western side of the constituency we have the gumbo plain, probably the best wheat country in Canada. I resided on the edge of that area. This legislation will be of little if any value to the farmers in that area. Whatever money they want to borrow, they can borrow from the banks. But they do not want to borrow today because, as I say, they do not like paying interest. They are already paying enough interest on their land holdings, machinery and so on. As they have the wheat, they feel they should be able to sell it and so pay off their obligations. If they want to borrow from the banks, they can borrow without this legislation.
Then we have the northern area of my constituency, around Stettler on the C.P.R. line. That is not such good land, but there is a greater rainfall there. I think the same
fMr. Quelch.l
thing applies to that area as to the western part of the constituency; it is a mixed farming area. Then you have an entirely different situation on the eastern side of the constituency. From Hanna east is what used to be known as the drought area of Alberta. This is where irrigation would be put in if the Red Deer diversion scheme were proceeded with. The government has been talking about that and making surveys for it since 1922, but the only time there is any real activity is just before an election, and I suppose next June there will be a great deal of activity there again. The farmers are still hopeful, however, that some day that program will be put into effect.
That is a dry area. Back in the years around 1919 or 1920 most of that land was sold for tax arrears. Most of the farmers got hopelessly into debt and the land was put up for sale. The mortgage companies did not consider the land worth sufficient to pay the reserve bid and so the land reverted to the provincial government. The provincial government realized that no farmer could make a living in that area on a half-section unit. Most of the land was taken back, and then any farmer who had a quarter or half section in that area was allowed to lease from the government about 2,000 acres. The units in that area are about 2,000 acres per farmer. They had to own one-quarter sections.
Just because a farm is large it does not mean that the farmer is in a position where he can borrow all the money he needs. As a matter of fact, the farmers in that area-all those big farmers-until recently, at least, were never able to go to the banks and borrow much money. Indeed, that area was blacklisted, and the farm loan board refused to make loans in that area. I have received many protests and have taken them up with the farm loan board, which has insisted it has not blacklisted the area but has judged each application on its merits and found the situation does not warrant making loans in that area.
However, in the past four or five years we have had heavy rains in that area and, generally speaking, there have been good crops for the past five years and these farmers are getting on their feet. Four or five years ago the average yield in that area was only six or seven bushels to the acre. During the last few years it has been about 16 or 17 bushels to the acre.
I want to relate that situation to this bill, because there you have large farms with fair yields of wheat, about 16 bushels to the acre. Take a farmer in that area getting a loan under this proposal. I do not say he would

not get a loan. He might get a loan of $1,500. What is the situation in which he finds himself if he takes a loan under this bill? We shall say, for example, that a two-bushel quota is put into effect and that the farmer has six or seven hundred acres of cultivated land, which would be a very moderate holding in that area. Many of the units are 2,000 acres, because it is considered necessary for a farmer to have that amount of land to make a living. At one time a farmer there was allowed to carry only three head of livestock on a quarter section, but that has been changed a little owing to the rains in recent years.
When a two-bushel quota is put into effect, that farmer takes a load of wheat to the elevator agent and asks what grade he can get. Probably there will be a dispute between him and the elevator agent, and the agent may say it is 4 while the farmer will say, "It is a good 3, and I am not going to take 4." What can the farmer do in a case like that, unless he is prepared to sell it for what the agent says he will pay? He will have to put that wheat into storage and a sample will be sent to the head office. Then the grade is sent back, and he is paid on that grade.
However, under this act he is not allowed to put that wheat into storage. Therefore, any farmer who has borrowed under this legislation, and who in order to get a fair grade tries to put his wheat into storage until such time as a grade has been arranged, puts the elevator agent in the position where he can be prosecuted if he allows the grain to be stored.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say, if I may, that the department has taken cognizance of that fact and an amendment will be offered if and when we get the bill into committee which will make it possible to put grain in storage. In the 1951 legislation there was a reason for that provision but in this legislation there is no similar reason and that restriction will be removed.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am certainly glad to hear that, because that was one of my very strong objections to the bill. Then there is another objection. The minister will probably say this one is not quite so well founded. He will probably say the provision is necessary, but I can tell the minister that it is going to be bitterly resented.
Take two farmers who are living side by side. I am speaking from experience in this case; it is something that has happened many times. Two farmers are living side by side and one is hailed out 100 per cent. What happens in a case like that? If his neighbour
Grain
has a good crop the practice in the past has often been for the farmer with the good crop to lend his neighbour who has been hailed out maybe a thousand bushels of oats, barley or wheat. I have done it myself, and I have had grain lent me.
The farmer who gets the grain and has no money can deliver the wheat on his own quota and sell it. Sometimes he makes a dicker with the farmer from whom he got the wheat and pays some of the money to him. If any farmer does that under this legislation he can be fined $500 and, if the hon. member for Prince Albert is right, he can land in jail. If the farmers find that out they will be hopping mad, because it is very often the only way they can help themselves.
I think the minister will agree that is a fine co-operative spirit, and nothing in this legislation should allow that fine co-operative spirit to be destroyed. The farmers help themselves.
I do not believe that anywhere in Canada you will find a better co-operative spirit that you will find amongst the farmers of the west. If one gets in bad shape his neighbours help him out if they can.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
May I ask a
question? What would happen if that cooperative spirit extended to the transferring of all the grain from one farmer to the other?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, the minister sees one ship and he talks about a fleet. I am not suggesting that at all. Remember that the farmer can only get a loan of up to 50 per cent of the amount of wheat. The minister knows that in many cases the farmer will have far more than the amount of wheat needed to cover the loan. Therefore it should be possible in a case like that for the farmer to transfer some of that wheat to a neighbour if he so desires.
Under the legislation he pledges so much of that wheat. He tells the bank manager how much wheat he can deliver and the price he expects to get, but so long as he states a certain amount of wheat and a price and the bank manager agrees to that, then any wheat the farmer holds in excess of that amount should be his property to do what he likes with. If he wants to lend a thousand bushels to his neighbour who has been hailed out there should not be any danger of that man being prosecuted or thrown in jail. At least the legislation should be wide enough to allow a certain amount of discretion so that the farmer can discuss the matter with the bank or with the wheat board and get permission for that transaction.
The minister knows that the situation today is difficult. We will not talk about who is to blame for the situation, but we are faced with

Grain
a situation today and it is a difficult one. Therefore anything the farmers can do among themselves to try to relieve the situation, to try to relieve the pressure, is something the minister should be glad to help them to do. I hope the minister can say the same thing about that provision as he said about the other one, that an amendment will be moved to modify its operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: May I say that if my hon. friend will draw up the amendment the government will consider it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I hope I have said enough to the minister to make him realize there are certain features of the bill that the farm organizations should be allowed to discuss. Therefore I again ask the minister to reconsider his decision not to allow the bill to go before the standing committee on agriculture. Let the bill go before the committee and call representatives from the farm organization. If they are able to make worth-while suggestions to the government and the government is prepared to accept those recommendations we may then have a bill that we will be able to support in the house. If the minister will pledge himself to send the bill to the agriculture committee after second reading, even now we will support second reading and vote against the amendment; but if the minister is going to stand by the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) that the bill will not be sent to that committee, then we will be obliged to support the motion of the C.C.F. for the six months' hoist.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to detain the house very long. The only reason I am speaking is that something was said last night by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) to which I wish to refer. As found at page 1268 of Hansard he said:
While we are on this point, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. I just wonder what organizations at the Saskatoon conference had wanted to take bank loans. I wonder whether the hon. member for Rosthern could inform hon. members of the house what organizations at that conference asked for bank loans. Was it the wheat pool? Was it the Saskatchewan farmers' union? The hon. member for Rosthern is not able to name one Saskatchewan farm organization which at that conference came out for bank loans.
I had said that organizations at that conference had suggested bank loans and that legislation like that of 1951 was the solution to this temporary difficulty. Apparently that was not believed by some hon. members opposite. Therefore I obtained the record of that meeting as kept by the secretary, and I looked over the record. I have thereby refreshed my memory on the matter, and I am going to give

the stand taken by some of the people representing organizations at that conference. Anyone who wants to check this can see the record in the hands of Mrs. Norman because as the conference went on she kept notes of what everybody said.
When this matter came before the conference on the afternoon of September 27, 1955, one of the first speakers was Mr. Wesson, who first of all dealt with the statistical position and gave various statistics. This is Mrs. Norman's record of what he said:
The shortage of cash was the problem. Wheat pool opposes advances of wheat board through elevators. Propose we ask federal government through parliament pass the same act as in 1951, advance through banks and guaranteed by federal government. Bank advance loans on the basis of the security of grain stored on the farm. Don't believe it should be interest free but some arrangement made by government through Bank of Canada making available to farmers at between 2J per cent and 3 per cent. This he felt would help to solve the immediate situation of farmers to help pay for urgent pressing financial bills.
At that point the conference recessed. I wonder what those members have to say who sneered and jeered and said that nobody had suggested bank loans, that everybody there was in favour of advance payments by the wheat board. Then I come to Mr. Schulz, the chairman of the interprovincial farmers' union and his attitude to the suggestion of Mr. Wesson, the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. This again is Mrs. Norman's record:
Mr. Schulz continued debate on Mr. Wesson's proposal. He stated he was in favour of Mr. Wesson's proposal but suggested that the government should absorb all interest.
Mr. Forsythe of Alberta chamber of commerce observed that about 20 per cent of Alberta machinery was sold through finance companies. His organization was proposing farm loans of long term and interest no higher than bank loans to their provincial government.
Mr. Barber of the Winnipeg labour council stated his council had passed a motion requesting that farm loans be advanced to farmers interest free.
Then my friends across the way stated that there was never any suggestion of farm loans.
Mr. Forrest of retail merchants association expressed the opinion that this was a recurring problem in recent years. Suggested that advances of half the value of the grain be advanced so that banks are repaid on a bushel basis as deliveries are made rather than in a lump sum. Felt there should be a concession in the interest rate as well.
Mr. Hansen submitted a table outlining the average purchasing power of wheat over a series of years. He felt also that other alternatives should be explored. Any plan considered should also be considered in light of practicability in future years.
Mr. Appleby-

Grain
He used to be president of the farmers' union.
__felt there must be supervision on when bank
loans are repayable which he felt should not be left to the discretion of the banker.
Mr. McFarlane of United Grain Growers outlined a plan of cash advances designed to be handled on the quota books through banks up to 50 per cent of grain he has on hand at a rate of 4 per cent interest.
The Manitoba government through their minister of agriculture indicated as follows:
Both plans suggested by Mr. Wesson and Mr. McFarlane would meet their approval . . . Interest rates he believed should be lower than in past.
Mr. Douglas of the Saskatchewan teachers association felt that bank loans might prove unpopular. He suggested advances to farmers through elevators. He thought there should be an interest rate of 3 or 4 per cent to discourage borrowing by farmers who weren't really in need.
There is there a reference to loans repayable with interest. Yet we were told that loans were never suggested.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Socialist political acrobats.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Then here is something which was said by Mr. Nollet, the provincial minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan:
If the Bank of Canada was able to loan money to banks to loan to farmers, it should also be able to loan money to the Canadian wheat board for loan to farmers.
We were told by the C.C.F. there never was any thought at the conference of loaning money to farmers.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Do it through the wheat board, not through the banks?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I suggest that I be permitted to make my statement. Then the hon. member can ask questions afterwards if he wishes to do so. I continue:
Mr. Brownlee . . . expressed the opinion that other problems in grain marketing must be considered. Looking upon the problem as an emergency, supplemental to bank loans municipalities must be engaged on a basis whereby they can advance money to farmers on the backing of government loans. This would spare the small farmer from being left without recourse if bank loans were refused and would be convenient to those farmers who live great distances from banks.
In other words, he said that it is quite all right to pass the legislation but this further provision should be passed supplemental to it.
Later:
. . . Mr. Brownlee stressed the need that advances must be placed on a business basis and not as a charity.
Later:
Mr. Hogg suggested that the resolutions committee consider the following resolution:
"Move we request advances on grain up to 50 per cent stored on farms and loaned through banks guaranteed by the dominion government at low rates of interest."
This was a resolution put before that conference.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It was not passed.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
A resolutions committee was set up to bring in a resolution. They brought in a resolution. There was an amendment moved to it. According to the notes the motion was as follows:
(In favour of principle of advances being made and made immediately)
Wesson-50 per cent of wheat.
Appleby-75 per cent of initial payment.
That is, Mr. Wesson thought it should be 50 per cent of the wheat and Mr. Appleby thought it should be 75 per cent of the initial payment. Mr. Brownlee thought it should be a flat maximum rather than "up to half".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask what was the motion, just for information.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I will give it to you in a minute. Then on the question of the dominion-provincial conference:
That this be presented to three prairie governments at once and they take it to Ottawa.
The question was whether it would be through the banks, through the wheat board or have the government set up a fund and administering it through a body, perhaps the municipalities. That is from Mr. Brownlee's remarks. An amendment to the amendment was moved by Mr. Schulz, seconded by Mr. Waldbauer:
Advance payments without interest when this is an emergency.
The amendment was that they delete:
-at a normal rate of interest not to exceed 3 per cent-
This was to the resolution as brought in by the resolutions committee. That rather sounds as though they were talking about loans. As this resolution committee brought in the recommendation for the resolution it contained these words:
At a normal rate of interest not to exceed 3 per cent.
The amendment was moved that these words be struck out and the amendment to the amendment was that the words "interest free" be substituted. That amendment to the amendment was defeated, that it was to be interest free. Then the amendment was carried that they strike out the reference to interest. Then the resolution which was brought in and has been cited in the house was passed. I just wanted to lay that before

Grain
the house so the house can judge who was telling the truth about that Saskatoon conference.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member for Rosthern, before he takes his seat, would answer the question I was going to ask and which he did not allow me to ask when he was speaking. maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I said that I had a vivid recollection of what took place at that conference.

speechtext: So have I.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That resolution was questioned; some hon. members here said they were there and that they knew what took place, that there was no question of loans, nobody had said anything about loans and so on. What I have given to the house are excerpts from those notes which she made as people spoke.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to speak on this occasion, but the two speeches that have been made from the opposite corner of the house

I refer to the one we have just heard and the previous one by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon)-make it necessary for me to say a few words. First of all, referring to the document from which the hon. member for Rosthern has just quoted, may I say that it is quite obvious that what he is quoting from is a set of notes made by one person at the conference. It is not a stenographic record. I asked him whether it was signed by the chairman of the conference. He did not answer that question, so I assume it was not signed by the chairman. We can therefore accept it only as being the opinion of the person who made those notes as to what transpired there.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I suggest that the hon. member certainly cannot rest his case on a set of notes drawn up by someone who is expressing from memory what transpired at this conference.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Just to correct my hon. friend, may I say this. This person whose notes I cited was duly elected secretary of that conference and made the notes at the time of the conference.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am not disputing for a moment that the person referred to was elected as secretary for that conference. I am pointing out, however, that this is not a stenographic record of what took place. My friend the hon. member for Rosthern is in the legal profession, and he knows that if he attempted to present evidence which was contained in a set of notes which he could not identify and which he could not prove as being correct, he would not get very far.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: He has identified them.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: He has identified the person who made the notes. But everyone knows that if he is going to use a document and assert it to be a correct record of what took place, that document should be signed by the chairman of the conference. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: He was present.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I was present also.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Many others were present also.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I would accept his notes if he would read the rest of them.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am very glad to have that question-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: -particularly from the hon. member who is so voluble. maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, the resolutions which have been used in regard to that conference are signed by Mrs. Bernice Norman, secretary of the interprovincial farm union council, and were not signed by the president.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is quite characteristic-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
It is quite characteristic of the hon. member for Rosthern to begin talking about something different. I was talking about the notes he used and he is trying to bring in the resolutions; that was not the

Grain
subject under discussion. The subject was these notes he used which are not signed by the chairman of the conference and are not a stenographic record of the conference; that is all I am saying. So far as the resolutions are concerned, no one is disputing the resolutions or the wording of them. I say he should rest his case, if he has one at all, on the resolutions themselves and not on what one person at the conference set down in her notes as her interpretation of what she heard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Pretty weak.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
If these hon. gentlemen want to chip in every few minutes with interruptions while I am speaking, I may tell them there is still plenty of time left for them to speak.
As I said at the outset, I rose to comment particularly on the contribution that the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine made to this debate. During his speech he made a couple of rather astounding statements. He asked the question, and he repeated it later when he interrupted the hon. member for Acadia, why should the farmers be paid for what they have produced and what has not yet been sold? That question in itself indicates a lack of understanding of this whole issue. I hope the hon. member is not speaking on behalf of the farmers of eastern Canada. Certainly if he is, he is doing a tremendous amount of harm to their cause.
In the first place no one in this house has asked that the grain producers generally be paid for all their production. The farmers themselves have not asked for that. They have asked for an advance of approximately half of what they expect normally to deliver, and that is a long way from what they have produced, as the figures are there to prove. The question indicates the hon. member does not understand the permit book. He does not understand the quota system. He does not understand that farmers are not asking, nor are the representatives of the farmers, that they be paid cash for all the grain they have produced, even though that is what is being done in the United States. We have heard time and again from the members on the other side that the farmers in Canada are being very well treated in comparison with the farmers in other countries. But if the government applied the same method that is being applied in the United States, then they would pay the farmer for all his production and in addition to that would pay him for storing the grain on his farm.
All the farmers are asking, and all we in this group are asking, is a long way from that. We are asking that they be given the opportunity to obtain an advance on a portion of
the quota that they are able to deliver under the present set-up. That is an entirely different thing from the interpretation the hon. member gave to it. But let us follow that a step further. If this parliament were to accept, heaven forbid, the philosophy that farmers should not be paid for what they have produced until it is sold, where does that leave our whole Agricultural Prices Support Act? Where does it leave the support price under butter and the support price under eggs? Where does it leave all these support prices which have been accepted as part and parcel of the agriculture policy? If the government, in a moment of weakness, were to give in to the advice of the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine it would mean the complete destruction of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. He is doing a distinct disservice to every dairy producer, every producer of eggs, not only in western Canada but in his own constituency. I think on reflection the hon. member would want to withdraw that statement and apologize for having made it.
He goes on to say that this bill is a privilege. He wonders why the farmers are dissatisfied with the present bill because it is a privilege. This privilege is an opportunity for the farmer to go further into debt, an opportunity to pay interest on money that is properly coming to him. I am not at liberty to refer to the clauses in the bill, but it is well known that one of the privileges in it is that if a farmer should happen to misunderstand one of the multifarious forms that have been drawn up, forms that were drawn up before this bill has passed, he can be fined $500. In addition to that penalty he would have to pay the amount of money still owing on his loan. I suppose that in default of paying his fine he could be imprisoned; that is the kind of privilege that is being offered under this bill.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We could discuss the clauses of the bill in committee.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I hear some chirping from the hon. member again, and perhaps if he would stand up and ask his question I could answer it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I was just suggesting that we could discuss the clauses of the bill when we are in committee.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I was discussing the motion that is before the house, and if the hon. member had done the same thing when he was on his feet he would not be getting into difficulty. He made a few remarks, too. He said, "My farmers are objecting to the payment of interest on advances to grain producers". Now, there is an indication of the

Grain
kind of ideology that exists in the minds of some Liberal members. He refers to "my farmers". Is that not a return to the feudal system? He speaks of his farmers. He has become the great white father of his constituency. Out west we take a rather different attitude, regardless of party. We feel we are the representatives of the people, not the owners of the people in our constituency. Here this hon. member stands up and says "my farmers object".
If we may follow that one step further, I wonder if he is doing a service to the farmers of eastern Canada by taking that attitude or-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am just stating what they think.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: -by proclaiming that his farmers are objecting to paying any interest that might be involved in this transaction if cash advances were being made. Let me remind him that we also represent farmers. 1 have no doubt I represent a good many more farmers than he does. The farmers in my constituency and in the prairie provinces have been helping to pay freight assistance on feed grain coming to his farmers and the farmers in other constituencies for a period of 12 years.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Are you suggesting that that be dropped?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: This has amounted to over $100 million. We are not objecting to it. We have been glad to give a helping hand.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Because you get the benefit, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It helps the western farmer, too.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I do not mind one at a time, but I think it gets confusing when we have more than that. We have never objected in this house to this freight assistance being paid because we felt it was part of the agriculture policy-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Because it helps yourself.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: -and because it is for the good of the nation as a whole. But there are those from eastern Canada who-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Does the hon. member think the freight subsidy on feed grain coming from the west to the east does not help the western farmer also?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is not the question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
At no time have I or any member of this group claimed that it does not help the western farmer. If it is of any assistance in the selling of feed grain then, of course, to that extent it is of some assistance to agriculture generally. But the point is, it is a direct subsidy to those who feed that grain in eastern Canada. Yet there are hon. members from eastern Canada who rise in their places and-I have no doubt without consulting the farmers at all-they take the stand that they are their farmers and they speak for them without consulting their opinions at all. They say that their farmers are objecting to something that may be of advantage to the grain producers who are willing to pay their share of freight assistance to ship the feed grain to eastern Canada.
All we are asking is that the members from eastern Canada take a fair and reasonable stand on this question. I think if they would only stop to think they would realize that in many ways the people of western Canada have been instrumental ever since confederation in subsidizing to a very great extent the people of eastern Canada in the form of tariff duties, for example. Every day that goes by hundreds of thousands of dollars are paid out by the people of western Canada to help to protect industry in eastern Canada. If they would stop to think of that I am sure they would take a little more reasonable attitude than they are taking on this question.
However, the question that is before us is whether this bill should be read a second time. We have stated, I believe in clear and unmistakable terms, that we are not prepared to support the bill on second reading. The other opposition parties have also indicated now that they will not accept the bill on second reading. We are basing our stand not only on what is contained in the bill, bad as it is, but also on the opinions as they were expressed in convention by the major farm organizations in western Canada.
Regardless of what the hon. member for Rosthern may say, regardless of how he tries to twist around what happened at the Saskatoon conference, regardless of what other members of the Liberal party may try to say, if they were to go out to western Canada today and test public opinion on this question I am sure they would come back quite convinced that this bill is not the answer to the problem. What is more, they would come back convinced that they are making a major mistake by assuming that just because at one time or another one, two or three of the leaders of some of the farm organizations made certain statements which make it appear as though they are supporting the bank loans, they were in fact speaking for the farmers

of that organization, because subsequent events proved that that was not so.
If the government feel so stubborn about this question, if they feel so sure of their position, I for one am prepared to let them test public opinion on this issue. Let them call an election tomorrow and actually find out the feelings of western Canada on this question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious from the nature of the discussion taking place on this bill today that we are dealing with a very complex problem that has a very serious impact on the general economy of Canada, and more particularly on the whole economy of the prairies. I am taking advantage of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) to lend my support to the suggestion that this particular piece of legislation be given the six months' hoist. I do so because I have considered the matter quite seriously as it would affect my own area, and I can quite readily come to the conclusion that nothing would be lost, so far as assisting the critical cash shortage among the farm population of my particular constituency is concerned if this legislation is never passed.
The last time I contributed to the discussion I emphasized why the bill is not wanted by the farmers of my area, and why if passed it will do nothing to solve the basic problem. The hon. member for Rosthern has been recapitulating certain arguments that have been made in the house. I would like to suggest, in refutation, an up to date point of view representing a cross section of the prairie farm population, a point of view, as a matter of fact, which was expressed to the government no later than yesterday, February 16. The interprovineial farm union, council delegation appeared before the government at that time, as they have appeared before other groups in this house, and repeated in no uncertain terms, verbally as well as in their written statement, that they favour the cash advance principle rather than the legislation that we have before us today.
We have had contributions from members from other parts of the country as well as from western Canada. As I have listened to the contributions from members from eastern Canada, I have been amazed. Some of those contributions have been formal speeches; others have been interjections. I have been amazed, Mr. Speaker, at the lack of understanding of the difficulty with which the farm population, the wheat grower especially, is faced at the moment. I refer particularly to the interjection of the hon. member for the Iles-de-la-Madeleine and others
Grain
who interjected, who feel that the legislation before us is in the form of a subsidy to the grain growers on the prairies.
I endeavoured to point out the other day that at no time has the prairie farmer ever been subsidized by any part of the Canadian economy. There is the misunderstanding that the operations of the Canadian wheat board involve a form of subsidy. But, as I emphasized the other day-and 1 repeat it this afternoon because the point does not seem to have penetrated-the farmer has paid out of the returns received from the marketing operations of the wheat board for every penny that he received. He has never been subsidized by the federal treasury. And of course the bill we have before us places him in the same independent position.
The point we are making is that the principle enunciated in the bill does not begin to meet the situation in which the farmer finds himself at the moment. It would seem that not only is there failure on the part of members from other sections of Canada who have intervened in the debate to understand the nature of the problem, but it would appear that the administration itself, the ministers most concerned, also fail to appreciate fully the nature of the problem.
I am going to deal with only one phrase in the bill which tends to emphasize the point I have just made. The bill refers to the cash shortage problem as a temporary financial difficulty. One reason I have opposed the legislation is that I feel this is not a temporary situation. If it were a temporary and passing situation no doubt the piece of legislation we have before us today would suffice, but it becomes increasingly obvious with the passing of time that the farmer himself regards the bill as quite ineffective to meet the problem. Certainly the fact that the government have described the bill as meeting a temporary situation indicates that they are almost completely unaware of the real nature of the problem.
Actually there has always been a shortage of cash among the farmers of western Canada. Until 1930 the farmers there operated largely under a subsistence economy. They did not have much to do with the exchange of money in any shape or form. They were suspicious of banks and the whole monetary scheme of things. I think this fact is dramatically demonstrated in the new forms of political expression which have emerged in western Canada. All of them have had as a basic part of their ideology some emphasis on the suspicious attitude toward the existing financial system. Farmers had got themselves into a situation of debt during the thirties, and that only increased their anxiety.

Grain
More recently because of changing circumstances the farmer has been moving toward a cash economy. Whereas he had been able to get along reasonably successfully on a subsistence basis, living as far as possible from the production of his own farm, today he is dependent upon money whether he likes it or not. He must have ready cash in order to meet current operations of his farming business. This is not a new situation, it is merely something which has come to a head because of the rapidly changing circumstances since the war, particularly in the past three or four years. It seems obvious that the government has failed to appreciate the nature of this problem.
One reason the situation has become critical from the standpoint of the Canadian farmer is the changing agricultural situation in our neighbour to the south. If we fully appreciated the change in the production and marketing of wheat we would readily come to the conclusion that we are faced with more than a temporary financial situation. Statistics are available so that he who runs may read. For example, we see that today the United States is producing annually more than 1,000 million bushels of wheat, whereas before the war it produced on the average some 700 million bushels of wheat. We must appreciate the difficulty facing the Canadian wheat economy because of that changed situation.
The consumption of wheat remains pretty well static. It is a well known fact that the demand for wheat remains practically stationary regardless of the level of production. When there is an increased level of production the demand remains almost static. The total world demand for wheat has grown ?ery slightly in relation to the total increase in world population. Domestic consumption in the United States has remained fairly static; therefore they have had to turn to the export market. Ever since the Canadian west was settled the export market traditionally has been largely taken care of by the wheat producers of the Canadian prairies. During the 10-year period 1930-39 the United States producers exported 59-9 million bushels, whereas for the comparative 10-year period 1946-55 they exported 309-3 million bushels. Such an increase would tend to suggest that somebody is going to suffer in the markets of the world and unfortunately that somebody has been the western Canada wheat producer.
It is equally obvious that the United States is going to remain a sharp competitor of the prairie grain producer, so that the cash shortage referred to as a temporary financial shortage is not going to decrease within the

foreseeable future. Actually Canadian exports have decreased proportionately in the past three years. We maintained our position fairly well up until the end of the war in Korea, but since that time Canada has been occupying a declining position in the export markets of the world. That problem has been intensified by the fact that there has been no real positive action on the part of the government to improve our exports.

Mr. Speaker, although this is the 29th day of the session, this is the first opportunity members have had to discuss the divorce bills which are before us, and I should like to say a few words on this particular case.
I would draw attention to the fact that we have only 60 minutes to discuss the 90 cases which are before us, and it would not be possible to give these bills the careful consideration Their Honours the senators did, but I have been interested in noting that several of the new senators have been working most carefully on these assignments, and on this one in particular. I notice that Senator Croll, in the first case that came before him, asked:
Q. Now at this stage you have said that three months after you were married your troubles started?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. How long did you know your wife before you were married?

There was a real attempt by His Honour the senator to try to find out what had gone wrong in this particular case. Another point I should like to mention is that we still find contradictions in the evidence given by these paid detectives. I would suggest to Their Honours in the other place, and to the committee that will be reviewing these cases, that careful consideration be given to the hired detectives who come here. One of these detectives reported that he and the other gentleman went to a particular place at a very unreasonable hour. One swore that the door was open without any question, and the other swore that before the door was opened the question was asked as to who was there and he replied that the clerk was there. I think it is significant that a detective giving evidence is prepared to admit-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not the Clerk of the house.

No, not the Clerk of the house. It was the clerk of the hotel in question. It seems strange that a detective who admits having given false evidence is able to give evidence in connection with a case of this sort and it is accepted. Senator Croll, naturally, considering it was his first case, was not quite familiar with the procedure. At page 14 of the evidence he is recorded as saying, after hearing the detective:
All we have at the moment is that two people were found in the room.
Her Honour Senator Hodges came to his assistance by pointing out:
We usually have a description of the room.
That was placed on the record. Senator Croll inquired:
Q. What day of the week was the 17th March?
A. A Thursday, sir.
I do not know what that had to do with it, but that was the evidence. I do not think we should call for a recorded vote on this particular bill, but I did want to make those few comments.

It is not fair to a respondent. We have a lot of these cases like this today, and it is getting worse. There was a time when the pleadings did give some particulars, but now they are coming here with just practically none.
A little later in the handling of the same case, Senator Roebuck as chairman of the committee said this, as recorded on page 12:
As to whether the evidence is sufficient we will discuss that afterwards. I am not satisfied. This is a professional investigator-
His name is Ernest Gordon Etheridge.
-and he did not go as far as he could have gone in giving us the best evidence that was available on that occasion. I say this now because we have heard these cases, and this investigator comes before us frequently. He ought to have gone on and found out from that man

got admissions from him as to who this woman was, and in his presence should have asked the woman who she was.
If my memory serves me correctly, the senators have had occasion to reprimand this same investigator on previous occasions, and here he is again coming before Their Honours with pleadings and with evidence which Senator Roebuck says are not satisfactory. It seems to me that Their Honours deserve credit for trying to get these investigators to take more care with respect to these matters; but it also seems to me, after reading a case like like this, that we in this house simply are not competent to decide whether or not this particular divorce should be granted.

Mr. Speaker, this is a rather unusual bill. In the

Private Bills'-Divorce
petition it is stated that the petitioner resides in the town of North Sydney, but when the case came before the subcommittee on January 17 it appeared that the petitioner resided in Montreal. The evidence does not make it quite clear how it is that in the one place it is stated that she resides in North Sydney and in the other place in Montreal. My learned friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre informs me that while this couple, when they were married and after they were married, resided in North Sydney, because the husband deserted and returned to Montreal his wife automatically became domiciled in the province of Quebec. This unfortunate woman has a tragic story as told in the Senate, and is put to the expense of coming to Ottawa to present her case.
There is another unusual feature in this case. The co-respondent appeared and gave evidence. It is obvious that this family has been broken and of course the customary questions were asked and answered with respect to whether or not there was any collusion. I think this is the first case of this particular type which I happen to have noticed this year, where the co-respondent has come before the committee, admitted the charges and a divorce has been granted.
When this case comes before the house committee I think there should be some discussion with respect to the information given in the petition as to the residence of this woman and the information given in the minutes of the subcommittee of January 14 setting forth that the woman is domiciled in the province of Quebec. The question should be cleared up whether a woman who has always lived in Nova Scotia and is deserted by her husband who goes to the province of Quebec should be put to the expense of coming to Ottawa to seek a divorce.

speechtext: I fully agree with the hon. member. As a matter of fact, I have been looking up some of the authorities and want to submit some observations to him. The hon. member concluded his remarks a moment ago by saying that he does not think members are competent to deal with these matters. No doubt he was referring to a bill he introduced the other day which will eventually come before the house, namely his proposal to refer this whole business, as he calls it, to the exchequer court. The hon. member almost said it without referring to the bill. I have heard him make remarks before with respect to this whole business and he will perhaps permit me to keep in my mind some of the words he does say in the house from time to time.
I want to refer particularly to the procedure that has been followed since five o'clock. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) have spoken to the second reading of some of the divorce bills that have been before the house today. In each of the cases on which they have spoken they have referred to the evidence taken in the Senate. I think they have both referred to members of the Senate who are members of that committee and who acted on it. I have in mind, in looking over these proceedings, that if we are to refer to the actions taken or the opinions expressed by the members of the other house, perhaps we are alluding to proceedings in the other house. That is something which is not allowed in this house. I would refer hon. members to citation 243:
Allusion to debates in the other house are out of order, and there are few orders more important than this for the conduct of debate and for observing courtesy between houses.
There was nothing derogatory in what was said about the members of the other place. As a matter of fact I think it was complimentary. 

Nevertheless I do not believe that in this house we should summarize the work that is being done by one or two individual senators in whatever work they are called upon to perform in the other house. Today, in view of the fact that the comments have not been derogatory, one might say, "Let it go". But tomorrow they may be derogatory and then I would be obliged to stop hon. members from referring to our colleagues in the Senate.
