speechtext: I do not rise to argue the point just now but would Your Honour regard what goes on in a committee or in a subcommittee of the other place as coming under the same ban that is stipulated in citation 243 which refers to the other house? The documents from which we have been reading are reports of proceedings in committees and subcommittees. They are not reports of what went on in the other house itself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member could also have asked whether it relates to debates. The citation to which I have referred, namely citation 243, refers to debates whereas the evidence that has been commented upon constitutes the proceedings in a working committee of the Senate.
Citation 243, although it refers only to "allusion to debates" is only one citation that points out the courtesy which must exist between the two houses. Generally speaking, I think there can be found other citations which are to the effect that in our own house in debate we should refrain from referring to individual members of the other place and what they have done, in whatever capacity, as far as their parliamentary work is concerned.
But there is this further point that I should like to submit to hon. members, namely the very nature of a private bill. When the second reading of a private bill has been given, its principle is to be accepted only conditionally. It is accepted conditionally upon the facts being proven before our own committee to which the bill must be referred. By our own standing orders we provide that, with respect to any private bill, the principle of it is accepted upon condition that it will be referred-we have no choice in the matter-to a standing committee where the facts relating to that bill will be proven. If the preamble is not proven, the bill does not go any further. But if it is proven, it comes back here.
I think the discussion of the evidence taken in the Senate is a premature discussion.

Private Bills-Divorce
Furthermore, to expect that hon. members, in debating the second reading of these bills, will make up their minds only upon the evidence taken in the Senate I think is prejudging what their attitude may be after they have looked at that bill in their own committee.
We know what the practice is and what it has been, but I am now talking about the theory of the whole thing. I am not assuming that our committee, let us say, will not meet -to take an absurd case-to consider these things or, even if they did meet, that they would not pass on them quickly because, let us say, they have confidence in what has taken place on the Senate side. At this moment this bill is to be referred to one of our standing committees. If hon. members wish to do so, they can call all the witnesses -including detectives when there were any- take their own evidence and make up their own minds.
Then in committee of the whole they can review the proceedings that have been reported from our standing committee. But at this moment, in discussing the principle of this bill on second reading, to summarize for the benefit of hon. members who perhaps, like myself, have not read the evidence, while at times it is extremely interesting and entertaining, I think it is something that does not meet the conditions that our rules prescribe.
I am not making a ruling today. I just want to submit these points for the consideration of hon. members. There is no question that, according to citations 769, 770 and 771, on second reading the principle of a private bill is accepted only conditionally. I read now from citation 769:
. . . but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.
The allegations of fact contained in this bill, as far as our own house is concerned, have not been proven. The allegations of fact in the petition have been proved to the satisfaction of the Senate before their committee, and they passed the bill and sent it to this house. But as far as we are concerned, we look at the second reading of this bill only conditionally, notwithstanding what the evidence might have been in the Senate. As far as we are concerned, the facts in connection with this bill have not been proven as far as our own committee is concerned.
Otherwise what would be the reason for sending these bills to our standing committee? You might as well have them dealt with
immediately-I am speaking of the bills to which hon. members have referred tonight- if they opposed them only on the basis of the Senate evidence but did not seek to do anything further in order to defeat them, such as provoking a division or anything like that. What is the purpose of sending them to our own standing committee? Why should they not go from here directly to the committee of the whole and be passed upon immediately? I consider that we are perhaps not adhering to procedure as strictly as we should in considering these private bills.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I say a word, Mr. Speaker, because I agree with Your Honour that perhaps the procedure we follow might be considered carefully. As a matter of fact, when I was thinking of what I would say if Your Honour gave me the floor for a moment, I was going to start off by agreeing with what you had said about second reading of a private bill being different from second reading of a public bill. In support of my agreement with Your Honour I intended to read the very sentence or two that you have just read from citation 769 of Beauchesne's third edition. Perhaps I might read the same sentence or two again:
A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.
However, Mr. Speaker, as I think you will readily realize, it was my intention not to stop there, as did Your Honour. I intended to go on and read the next sentence or two, which are as follows:
Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the house will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee.
This is the first occasion on which the bill is before the house otherwise than pro forma or in connection with the standing orders; and if the bill be opposed, upon its principle, it is the proper time for attempting its defeat.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I contend that if I, as one of the few members who may happen to have read some of these cases, feel that the principle of a particular bill, the principle of granting a particular divorce as between Mr. and Mrs. A., is objectionable and should not be agreed to, I am within my rights and within the rules of the house in speaking to that bill at second reading. Certainly I would be within my rights in attempting its defeat if I felt that such a bill should not be allowed to pass.	:

Private Bills-Divorce
I hope I was not mistaken if I detected in what Your Honour was saying-Your Honour was reading my mind so perhaps I can read Your Honour's-that Your Honour was almost challenging us to divide the house on some of these bills. Well, in the past we have tried and we have found, to our surprise, cases which we thought should be defeated, and knowing the views of many members in this house on divorce we thought would be defeated, which nevertheless were carried. Whether or not we seek to divide the house I suppose depends upon whether we think, having in mind the circumstances of a particular bill, we can win the majority of the members to our view that a particular bill should be defeated.
Nevertheless, because there are some divorces we think should not be granted, we believe we have the right to draw attention to the ones which in our view are slightly objectionable as we go along so that when we get to ones that are really objectionable we will be in a position to give the house an opportunity to divide on them.
As I say, I agree with Your Honour's contention that these bills are different from public bills. But there is a difference within the difference. As I have pointed out by referring to citation 769, where we think there are objections to a particular divorce, it seems to me that we have the right to discuss it on second reading. Nevertheless, I agree that the whole procedure might be reviewed. We would be glad to discuss it privately with Your Honour or in a committee. Indeed, as Your Honour knows, I would be glad to find some way whereby parliament might get rid of the whole business.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry if the hon. member detected in anything I have said a view that he could not discuss this bill on second reading. Of course if he feels the principle is objectionable, he will discuss it, and he should discuss it. Under the rules he will be quite in order. But in discussing the principle of this bill I consider that he does not necessarily have to refer to the evidence which has been taken on the Senate side. That is my point.
Suppose the bill were introduced in this house. When second reading was being considered in the Senate they would have no evidence whatever. They accept the principle conditional upon their committee proving the allegations of fact. We are in the same position here. I think if you take for granted that our objection to the bill should be based on the evidence taken in the other place, you do not attach very much importance to the ability of our own committee to prove the facts themselves.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I point out that in the case of a private bill coming before this house initially, other than a divorce bill, the same general rules apply. We expect the sponsor of such a bill to make an initial statement as to what is involved in that bill. I would be satisfied with the same practice in respect of these bills. If instead of our being given the evidence as a means of finding out something about them, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) or the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) who is sponsoring some of these bills on his behalf, would speak on second reading and tell us why he thinks we should submit this bill to the committee, as is done in the case of private bills, then I would say that would obviate the necessity of our looking at the evidence furnished to us.
I would be interested in what Your Honour has in mind when you say that a reference to the evidence is not necessarily desirable on second reading. I take it there is no question as to our right to refer to it if we wish. My point is that we are accepting this evidence as something that is given to us in lieu of a statement in support of the bill being made by the mover of second reading.

I wonder if I might make a comment on this. I would support what you have said, Mr. Speaker. I just point out to you that if the evidence is going to be allowed on second reading, and if we consider every bill that has been offered to the house at this time, it would take every hon. member 26J hours to read the evidence. He must be in the same position as my hon. friend to be able to debate a particular bill, and I do not think any hon. member, on this side of the house at least, has 26J hours to spend reading evidence on divorce bills.

I should like to draw to your attention the fact that during the last parliament when a divorce bill was brought before this house, a member on the government side objected to it being proceeded with because members had not received a copy of the evidence. Mr. Speaker upheld that objection at that time because members had not received a copy of the evidence and were therefore not in a position to proceed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member have the precise date of that incident?
No, I have not, but I know I am speaking correctly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I recall one, and in discussing this point with my predecessor he had doubts as to whether or not hon. members would

have the right to hold up a bill which comes up for second reading only on the ground that the evidence had not been received from the Senate. I think in this case one wants to accommodate all hon. members. I do not think I would, myself, care to have to render a judgment on that point, although I think if I were pressed I would do so. The Clerk informs me that the evidence is always received with the bill, so there is one copy of the evidence available. Copies are not always printed and distributed when the bill comes up for second reading.
In these instances today, all the evidence has been printed and distributed. When a bill is called, it is printed. According to our standing order all bills must be printed before second reading. They have been printed and they meet with our requirements; therefore I can put the question whenever they are called. Theoretically I do not believe hon. members may object on the ground that the evidence has not been printed and distributed. The evidence is not part of the bill.
As I say, I raised the point only as a matter of interest and perhaps as a diversion from the rather monotonous task I was performing of proposing one bill after another. Having done so, hon. members may consider what I have said. It is not a ruling, but I thought I would make these remarks in order to give hon. members an opportunity to think them over. Perhaps on some other occasion I may have to rule, but I want to go further into this myself.

I am not clear as to whether or not you consider it is permissible to refer to the evidence in connection with these cases. May I say that last year there were four or five cases before us which this house refused to accept on the evidence as it came from the other place; we reversed the decision. If we had not been able to refer to this evidence I am sure we would not have managed to win a favourable vote in the house. We have no other information on which to reach a judgment as to whether second reading should be given or refused, except on the basis of the material which is supplied to all hon. members reviewing the work of the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not want to make a ruling on this point; I have doubts. If the hon. member wishes to continue quoting from the evidence I will not stop him on this occasion.

speechtext: Can the hon. member for Skeena, who has been named as the mover of the motion for second reading of this bill, give any reasons why we should support it on second reading?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am particularly pleased that an opportunity has been given to me to express the reason. The hon. member for

Winnipeg North Centre will, 1 think, follow my line of reasoning. If he agrees with me that under certain circumstances, regrettable circumstances, in Canada, it is expedient that people be divorced, then he thinks as I. He and I will both have the greatest respect for those who believe that under no circumstances should couples be divorced.
In this case I, as sponsor of the bill, have reason to believe it can be proved that those circumstances justifying the passing of the bill will be proven or can be proven in our committee. They cannot be proven under the rules, I submit, until such time as the bill reaches the committee which has the power to look into those statements of fact. In other words, sir, the principle of the bill which we are now called upon to approve or disapprove is that if certain facts can be proved, then it is expedient that a divorce be granted. The application of that principle to a particular set of facts cannot be discussed by this house at this time because those facts cannot be made available in final form in this house for the house to take action on them until such time as this house has referred a private bill to a committee.
That is the point on which I was greatly tempted to rise to my feet a few moments ago, because I do feel that that is the basic principle in passing private bills on second reading. I do not know the history, but there has grown up in this parliament the practice of considering this class of private bills differently from others.
It was my privilege at one time to be quite vitally concerned with a contested private bill of another nature which started in the Senate and came to this house. It was most noticeable at that time that no evidence given in the committee of the Senate came to this house. Then there were a number of pipe-line bills a few sessions back which originated in the Senate, and no evidence came to this house upon which it could base approval of the motion for second reading. It was only the basic principle; and whether there was sufficient evidence to make that principle applicable could, I submit, be made known to this house only through the miscellaneous private bills committee or some other appropriate committee.

The fact is that a number of us, including the hon. member, Your Honour and others, will no doubt have private discussions about this matter because it is quite important. It does seem to me, if I may add this word, that what the hon. member for Skeena has said suggests that second reading in the case of divorce bills means something quite 67509-85J

As a member of Your Honour's committee which met for several sessions to deal with the rules and procedures of this house, if I may say so I am pleased with the job we did. Many of the changes we made have already proven to be very valuable and I think we cleared up many ambiguities with respect to the procedures of the house. I suppose this matter of divorce was a bit difficult for us to deal with effectively, but it seems to me that it is one piece of unfinished business, this question of how we should be handling these divorce bills.

C.B.C. DIRECTORATE
speechtext:
1.	Who are the members of the directorate of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation referred to by the minister in the House of Commons on February 7?
2.	How often does the said directorate meet?
3.	What are its duties?
Answer by: Mr. McCann:
On February 1, the hon. member for Eglin-ton asked if there is a directorate in the C.B.C. which concerns itself with whether a program will or will not go on the air. It was thought at the time that the reference was to one of the regular divisions or departments of the C.B.C. The reference and this inquiry is now understood to relate to some presumed special directorate or body that decides whether programs do or do not go on the air.
The C.B.C. advises that there is no such special body which considers and decides whether programs should or should not be
broadcast. The C.B.C. as a corporate entity has full and independent responsibility for all program decisions which are taken through the usual administrative process of chains of responsibility.

The house resumed, from Thursday, February 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 82, to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
Grain

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have read carefully, Mr. Speaker, your remarks at the conclusion of my address last night and I want to say that, as usual, you are absolutely fair and correct. Your assistants found it necessary to call me to order when you were absent from the chamber and they, too, were quite correct and fair. But in my defence I should like to say that members supporting the government had been so far from this subject that I felt without some reference to some of the remarks made it would have been interpreted that we accepted those views. I have discussed the remarks I propose to make this morning with my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and I will try to be absolutely on the beam all the way.
We are discussing Bill 82, which is an act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain. I am against that all the way. We do not want credit. We have had too much credit. We want to get fair consideration, nothing more and nothing less. This -is not a temporary situation. While the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has not taken any part in this debate I want to call him as my witness in saying that this is not a temporary situation. The Minister of Finance, speaking in New York, quite correctly said that this situation has been caused by policies in other countries. He also said that his government, the government of Canada, is concerned about the fact that wheat production is the principal source of cash income to the great majority of western farmers and his government was bound to be greatly influenced by anything so vital to them and to the whole national economy.
I want to make an appeal to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The Prime Minister has established, and has earned, the respect of a great many Canadians. I feel it is not fair for him to be in a position where the two senior members of his cabinet are so irresponsible in discussing this national problem. The Prime Minister is still the chief, and with all due respect to the contribution the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made in the past

and I am among the first to give him credit for the outstanding job he did during the war-if he were to approach this problem as he did his problems during the war, he would be saying the same sort of thing that the Minister of Finance is saying, that this is not a problem which has resulted from beneficent nature. It is a problem which results from policies which are not formed outside of Canada.

Grain
If we had had as minister of agriculture during the war a man who approached this problem as did the minister of munitions and supply at that time, our present Minister of Trade and Commerce, our farmers would not be in the position where they are so bitter as they are now. Therefore, I suggest to the Prime Minister that he deal with this problem in two stages; that he persuade his two senior members to take a holiday right now and go to Florida and have the Minister of Finance pilot this bill through the house, because I am sure the Minister of Finance would say that this is not a temporary problem. He would admit that it is a problem, and I am sure the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), whom we are glad to see back in the house this morning, would do as he did last summer, namely, take over agriculture during the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, and he would certainly do a much better job than the Minister of Agriculture in getting this piece of legislation discussed. I am sure that with the two senior members out of the country the cabinet would be prepared to accept the analysis made by the Minister of Finance in New York.
The farmers do not want too much. They merely want recognition of the facts as they exist and an indication that the government is prepared to do something about them. An act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
First of all I find that some of the subjects mentioned in the bill are a little difficult for me to follow. In the first place, I am of the opinion that the difficulty has not arisen particularly because of the farmer's inability to sell all of his grain. Certainly the difficulty has arisen because of the government's inability to sell the wheat of western Canada. It is not the farmer's job at all to sell this wheat. The government's policy should be so designed as to take care of the wheat of western Canada. The government has been solely responsible for the sale of wheat in this country. Therefore it is the government's responsibility now to see to it that the farmers are given assistance towards obtaining some cash in this time of emergency.
It is not my intention to establish need at this time, because I have already done that on another occasion during this debate and many members in the House of Commons have brought forth that very point. It has been well established by all soundthinking members that the western farmer is in need of assistance. I said that I thought the fact had been established by all soundthinking members in this house, but there are some members apparently who disagree with that point of view.

In view of the fact that the Liberal leader in the province of Alberta has come out and condemned this bill, I think it is about time some of the Liberal members from Alberta got up and made themselves known in this respect. Mr. Speaker, it is most understandable that I should be wholeheartedly in support of the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), since I on a previous occasion introduced an amendment which did not appear to meet with the approval of the government. It is obvious that the government members are becoming quite fed up with the debate on wheat. We are fed up with the legislation which the government is trying to introduce.

The members of the government had an opportunity to rid the house of the discussion on a previous occasion when I moved my amendment and if adopted the pros and cons could have been argued and debated before the agriculture committee. Had they followed that procedure they would have had an opportunity to consider the opinions of the farm organizations in western Canada, and the private members of the government from other areas of Canada would have been in a position to appreciate the problems which are confronting western farmers.
On previous occasions I have referred to the protest meetings which took place in Saskatchewan with respect to the introduction of this legislation and the manner in which it was introduced by the government. It was apparent at the time this legislation was mooted that the government gave no thought to getting the advice of western farm organizations, since their decision was already reached before the conference was held in Saskatoon and before the organizations had an opportunity to present a brief to the government. I might say that the brief that the organizations at that meeting presented to the government was watered down at the insistence of certain organizations which are entirely sympathetic to the government.
Some of those protest meetings took place in my constituency. On the last occasion I spoke on this measure I did not have the time to point out the fact that many of those organizations held their meetings spontaneously, at the insistence of various leaders within the community, who felt that a rank injustice was being perpetrated, and they did not want the whole procedure to go unnoticed and not be granted an opportunity to express an opinion. The Saskatchewan farmers' union played a very significant part in giving as much advice and assistance to these meetings as they could so that the farmers could be advised of the circumstances surrounding trade, circumstances that are resulting in the point directly related to the bill, namely, the financial difficulties of farmers. One of these meetings was held in my own community of Kindersley, where they had the good fortune of having the services of professor K. A. H. Buckley, of the University of Saskatchewan. After following such a procedure, after having information on a non-political basis, the farmers at that meeting, which was attended by over 100, passed a resolution to the effect that the emergency bank loans policy is inadequate for many producers. They requested interest-free cash advances on the basis of 6 bushels per specified acre. Similar

meetings were held at Swift Current, Mr. Speaker, and I understand the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) was in attendance at one of those meetings. I would suggest that in this debate he take the opportunity to outline the resolution which was passed at that grain marketing conference, since it is the people whom he represents who made the decision at that meeting. An obligation rests squarely on his shoulders to present their views before this house.
Meetings were also held at Kerrobert, Unity and Wilkie in my constituency. I may say that the resolutions from each meeting were very similar indeed. This can only mean one thing. It means that the farmers of western Canada have a unanimity of thought on this matter which perhaps they have not had on any other matter except on the insistence on the orderly principle of marketing through the Canadian wheat board.
We will find, Mr. Speaker, that the situation which originated at the time that the problem developed immediately after the harvest of 1955, is growing continuously worse. These protest meetings are still taking place in an effort to bring to the attention of the government the true situation which exists in western Canada, and which is confronting the people of that area. I am informed that even today farmers are making an effort to plow out their roads to town so they can meet together and discuss their problems relative to their financial position and their inability to market any grain at all.
As hon. members may know, we have had one of the worst winters in the west that we have had for many years. The snow and cold conditions are creating serious hardships among the farmers because of the added expense they must go to in an effort to keep their lines of communication open to get to town to buy their normal groceries, to have fuel delivered to their houses and to maintain the other aspects of daily living. The storm of December 12 was very significant. Along with a fairly heavy snowfall, the snow drifted around the farmsteads and buildings, and hon. members from other parts of Canada must appreciate what a great problem it must be to have to spend $100, $200, and much more than that in many instances, to keep the roads open so that one can carry on his normal day-to-day living, if not in comfort, at least in the position where he can get to market and get supplies periodically.
With that background information it is significant to note that farmers are today plowing their roads so that they will be in a position to discuss the very problem that

we are discussing here today. They are very disturbed, as they plow their roads to town, to pass by the piles of wheat which are left on the ground. It is particularly disturbing to them, Mr. Speaker, because they realized at the time they piled this wheat on the ground it was unsafe, it was unsatisfactory, but they had no finances to build any storage. Their credit was limited. Anyone from any part of Canada who has done any building realizes that the amount of money which is required to build any kind of a structure to house grain is quite large. Because of the backlog of debts which the farmers had already incurred it was impossible for them to incur additional expenses in building farm storage. It is therefore most heartbreaking for them to drive by these piles of wheat which are being consistently cast asunder by the winds, because a pile of wheat is a conglomeration of small kernels which can be readily lifted and blown away to be lost forever, and the farmer sees the return from his year's labour gradually shrinking before his eyes. In addition to that he will find that in the spring as the snow melts it settles around the pile of wheat which he has not had an opportunity of moving and his loss becomes greater.
Then as he goes by those piles of wheat on his way to town he realizes that there are 58 million bushels of storage space available in the terminal elevators. He recalls on December 7 the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stated at Edmonton that there were 100 million bushels of space available in the terminals. His exasperation then reaches the breaking point. He sees his wheat being drifted about and destroyed by the wind and he knows that there are 58 million bushels of storage space available. He knows that if the administration of this government had been efficient in all its aspects much of that wheat would be safe in the terminals rather than wasting away on the ground.
In view of the position of leadership which this government likes to take in terms of international affairs, it is a tragic contribution which they are making toward the support of underdeveloped and starving countries of the world when they let this wheat, which we know we will need in the future, be spoiled and rotted on the farms of western Canada when there is space available in the terminals.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) referred to the speech made by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy). I agree that the hon. member for Westmorland was ill advised to start off with the line of debate he did when dealing with a subject with which he was so unfamiliar.

1 must say that I do give credit to some of the government backbenchers who have come to me personally and asked for my views on the situation of the farmers in western Canada. Those hon. members have an appreciation of the problems which exist in western Canada.
We cannot for one minute assume that farm conditions in other areas are similar to Saskatchewan. There are many factors which must be considered and a comparison of similar circumstances is most difficult. I suggest to members of the government that they would indeed be well advised to invite the western farm organizations-I am thinking of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the interprovincial farm union council and other prairie pools-to send representations down here to discuss the problems with them so that they may become acquainted with those problems.
The attitude of Saskatchewan Liberals is most unreliable and it is because of that unreliability that many Ontario and maritime members have spoken to me. I appreciate that fact and I appreciate the attitude they have adopted after I have discussed the problem with them. Many times they have said to me that they did not realize that things were that bad, that a farmer might have been able to sell only 300 bushels of grain when he had 5000 bushels in store on his farm.
I would point out that one of the inequalities which exists is in the distribution of box cars among the marketing points in western Canada. It is pointed out in the wheat review that there are many marketing points in Saskatchewan which are still on the initial unit basis. That means that the farmers at those points are allowed to deliver only 300 bushels of wheat. At the same time it is significant to note that a number of points are on the 3-bushel quota.
This indicates to me that the transport controller has not been paying close attention to the problem. There is a dispatch in today's Montreal Gazette which indicates that the transport controller has stated that the grain will be moved before the Canadian wheat board has made an estimate as to how much grain it will want moved. According to this article the controller stated that there is no shortage of box cars holding up prairie grain shipments.
If there is no shortage of box cars holding up prairie grain shipments then the Minister of Trade and Commerce should be severely criticized for allowing a situation to arise whereby there are 58 million bushels of storage space available in the terminals. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) has

denied any responsibility for filling up the terminals, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated that the moving of the wheat was not his responsibility. Those two ministers would be well advised to get a little closer together and give some thought to the position of the farmers of western Canada who are supposedly being served by the transport controller.
It is fairly obvious that members on the government side who are not conversant with this problem are creating a serious break in relations between western and eastern Canada. Their determination to prevent the introduction of any legislation which would prove to be of material assistance to western farmers is doing much to undermine the co-operation which must exist between all farmers of Canada if we are to achieve our fair share of the national income.
I do not think you will find many farmers on the western plains who will begrudge the freight rate assistance being provided for Ontario farmers, who will begrudge the assistance given to the maple sugar producers to purchase aluminum equipment, or who will begrudge other forms of direct and indirect assistance which have been given to the farmers in this area. I think also that eastern farmers generally have a great deal of sympathy for the western farmer.
I am making the statement now that if the government members continue to try to make a breach between the farmers of Canada, if they continue to be ignorant of the conditions which exist in western Canada, there can be only one answer or only one solution. I have heard this discussed many times during the last few months in Saskatchewan.
The people of western Canada are becoming fed up with the attitude of the government in denying them the South Saskatchewan dam and other things which would improve conditions in western Canada, so much so that they are considering marching on Ottawa. I must say that some of them are thinking in terms of secession.
I submit it is a pretty tragic indictment of the government of Canada when one section of the country realizes that it has been ignored, that it can no longer expect to get consideration from the government. It may be that if this Liberal government continues in power for too many years the only alternative will be for the western provinces to devise their own form of legislation so that they can be treated as they wish to be.
The challenge is out. I do not think any hon. member of this house will agree that the work done many years ago to bring about a national Canada should be so easily wrecked

by the failure of Liberal members from the prairies to present to their colleagues the conditions which exist in western Canada, present them with insistence in their party caucus and before this parliament of Canada. The challenge rests with them and I hope we will not be disappointed.

I say to my hon. friend, in the last couple of days the farmers' union has made a submission and has set out in very careful detail the position of the gross and net farm income for all of Canada between 1951 and 1955, and also the gross and net income in the last several years. These statistics indicate the serious cash situation in which the farmer finds himself.
As far as Canada in general is concerned, starting with 1951, the gross and net income among farmers is set out as follows: In 1951 it went down by 10-72 per cent; in 1953, by 21-1 per cent; in 1954, by 48-2 per cent. The figures for 1955 will indicate a further reduction in net income. Net income, of course, is based on a relative comparison between gross income and the cost that the farmer has to incur in order to operate his farm. These costs are rising.
I now come to the gross and net farm income for the prairie provinces for the same period. In 1952 the net income was down by 3-13 per cent; in 1953, by 21-6 per cent; in 1954, by 66-64 per cent. The final 1955 figures are not yet available, but they will indicate a further decrease. A 66 per cent decrease in net farm income in a matter of three or four years is one which explains as clearly as possible the need of cash. If these figures were based upon the purchasing power of the dollar the condition of affairs would be even more serious than is apparent from the simple percentage statistics that I have placed before you, Mr. Speaker.

I quote from the 1951 legislation:
Where a person is convicted of an offence under this section there shall be imposed on him, in addition to any fine, a penalty equal to such amount of any guaranteed loan made to him in respect of which the offence was committed as has not been repaid by him, with interest thereon to the date of the conviction, and the penalty shall be paid to the bank-
If the farmer is proceeded against and fails to pay his fine, the alternative is jail. In addition to the fine there is also a penalty of the amount of the loan. I say that that type of thing is disgraceful legislation. If he commits an offence he immediately finds himself in the position of being subject, first to a penalty up to $500 and then in addition to be ordered to pay as a penalty the amount that he owes.

A very large crop had been grown but a great deal of it was tough and damp and a very large area was under snow and could not then be harvested. Faced with this situation, which was certainly very much grimmer than now prevails, the government introduced a bill to provide shortterm advances to farmers. The banks were to be guaranteed against losses on loan advances up to $20 million on both grain in storage and grain in the fields.

Is it any wonder that in 1951 the farmers did not accept that kind of legislation? They were not looking for passports to jail, they were looking for advances which would make available to them the necessary money to pay their current expenses.
What happened-I say this with great respect-to the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) a few days ago simply summarized the attitude of western farmers everywhere. As a matter of fact, if I might be allowed to paraphrase-

My right hon. friend will understand this because he was an American until recent years. Paraphrasing Emerson I would say: Here once the embattled farmers stood and fired their shots heard around the west. That represents the attitude of western farmers everywhere. They are demanding that cash advances be provided. The record before us indicates the extent of that demand.
If the legislation did not work in 1951 why embalm it in another piece of legislation which is almost a photographic copy except for the amount which the banks may lend and also the extension of the penalties provided in 1951. The reason given by the minister in 1953 was that this kind of thing could not be done because the farmers were dishonest, because they were evading it, and because we have suffered loss. Ever since 1951 whenever any member of the opposition has suggested that something should be done to assist the farmers by cash advances on farm-stored grain the minister has bravely stood his ground and pointed out that the 1951 experiment was unsuccessful, that it did not work, that only a very small percentage of the total amount guaranteed was taken over by the farmers.
That is the reason for the small amount. What is the percentage? I understand it is about 4 per cent of the farmers. Four per cent have taken advantage of this, and that is all. They have been forced into that position against their own wishes and desires, against the resolutions which they themselves joined in having passed.
That is the reason why we take the stand that we do, and it has been a consistent stand. Last September when the matter was first mentioned, with the approval and consent of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) I said that we believed in cash advances and that parliament should be called

together. When the Leader of the Opposition was in western Canada in October and November and saw the situation he reiterated over and over again the need for action along this line being taken. But parliament was not called. If parliament had been called, the whole matter could have been discussed. Instead of that, the back-door method of cabinet decree was used and we are asked in parliament to rubber-stamp what the government did when it acted in derogation to everything the western farmer has demanded.
I was surprised this morning to hear the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking) make a statement which in some ways seems to epitomize the viewpoint of some of my hon. friends opposite. Referring to the western farmers, he said this: "Your farmer will certainly do some work for a change."
That was a statement that ought not to have been made. I would like to see some of the Liberal members from Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta stand up and repudiate that-unless my hon. friend has indeed become the voice of the members of the province of Ontario supporting the government. That was a very serious statement. We are not asking for any handouts. The government is the only market, through the wheat board. The farmer is entitled to what he has earned. Being in that position, he resents having to pay interest on the work he has done. We took that stand first in September, then when our leader visited western Canada, then again in the initial speech made in this House of Commons this session by the hon. gentleman, and also during the month of December when we said, as far as the resolution stage was concerned, "We shall accept this, because apparently something is going to be done."
I say, with all respect to the Department of National Revenue, which seems to have a monopoly of this sort of thing, that what is produced is almost a photostatic copy of a bill that did not work then. We were defeated when we asked that it be submitted to the agriculture committee. What we are trying to do is to secure through parliament by parliamentary means what the western farmer is asking for and what he has demanded over and over again. It may be that in the stand we take, because of the overwhelming government majority, this legislation will be pushed through. If it is, my answer to those who push it through is that if the 1951 legislation does not work, this legislation cannot work either. The experience of the past few months and the degree to which it has not been made use of indicates that it does not meet the situation.

indeed, this problem is one that recurs from year to year. Not every year, but from time to time, it has recurred since 1952. In November 1953 the Leader of the Opposition, then speaking as I say he was speaking, for those in western Canada who had been asking for this kind of thing, demanded that legislation providing for cash advances should indeed be brought into effect. When finally the bill came up for second reading, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) showed the attitude of this party in the amendment he tried to move, but it was ruled out of order. That amendment-and I am now paraphrasing-provided that the bill be not now read the second time but that there be substituted therefor legislation to provide for cash payments on farm-stored grain. In other words, cash advances are what we in this party have demanded over and over again. The support we have given to them is indicated by what I mentioned a moment ago-our support of similar legislation in 1953 and since.
Apparently even among members of the government there was not very much certainty as to what they were going to do. You will remember when Mr. McDonald, the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan, came here-I think it was in October-and said something had to be done. He said, "I can't tell you what it is." It is like the old Indian medicine, Kickapoo juice; it would cure anything, but they never told you the contents. He returned and said, "I have found it; I have got it." Then it was rumoured that the plan was indeed guaranteed bank loans. On October 24, 1955, the Minister of Agriculture, speaking in Winnipeg, said that while there were complaints, including a complaint from the Manitoba government, these complaints were based on a belief that the federal government had chosen bank loans rather than advances. He said, in effect, "Don't believe it." There was the criticism of the Manitoba government and its representative. There has been the criticism of the leader of the Liberal party in Alberta, who knows what the people think.

I should correct that and say "western farmers". I have risen this afternoon to make one or two observations I have wanted to make for some time. I want to say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that the position in which western farmers have been placed by this situation is deeply resented by them. I informed the minister of a constituent of mine who for two reasons, one because he needed the storage space and the other because he needed cash, was actually selling 1954 feed wheat to the stockyards in Saskatoon for a cent a pound and paying 20 cents a bushel for hauling it. In other words, he was getting a net of 40 cents a bushel at Rosetown, Saskatchewan, for that wheat. When you examine the value of the dollar today compared with what it was in the 1930's, about which we have so often talked in this house, that means that in pre-war currency he was getting about 19 cents a bushel or about the lowest price that farmers in that area got for their wheat at the elevator in the very depths of the depression.
I am not going very fully into the legislation before us this afternoon because it has been gone into by so many. It is unsatisfactory legislation. It is legislation which we

Grain
saw introduced in 1951 and which we opposed at that time by an amendment to the resolution urging the government at that time to adopt a policy of cash advances. That has been our plea in the house ever since 1951. I am going to say to the minister that I am not in agreement with those who say that because we have a surplus of wheat at the moment on the western prairies our farmers should be told to cut down their production of wheat next year. I am not sure when that wheat will be needed in view of the reports coming to us from Europe at the present time that hundreds of thousands, yes, millions of acres of winter wheat have been destroyed by the great frost in Europe. Next year, or the year after this, wheat may be a very valuable asset to Canada and to the world.
I am never one of those who believe in restricting production to meet a situation of this sort, but I am saying that this valuable reserve, this valuable asset to Canada and to the world should not be carried by the farmers who produced it but that the people who should carry the burden are the people of this dominion. Of course it can be done in two ways, by making cash advances repayable when the wheat is marketed on a quota basis and then the surplus stored and storage paid to the farmers who have their wheat properly stored to meet the future needs of people here and across the world.
As was said this morning, because of the inability of the farmer to market his grain and his inability to get cash advances which would enable him to build more adequate and safe storage space, there has been a serious deterioration of wheat on the western prairies which we as a nation and the world may regret in the days to come. I have never had very much faith in the government's protestations about the wheat board. I am very glad that recently in the debate we have not heard it said that those of us on this side of the house are weakening or undermining the wheat board. That can be demonstrated to be quite untrue. As a matter of fact the records clearly prove on which side of the house the people sit who through the years have been supporters of the orderly system of marketing.
I regret that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is not in his seat this afternoon. Last night he accused me again of having misrepresented him on many occasions over recent years. This matter of policy has been discussed before not only in this house but throughout the country. The government has carried on with a voluntary system for five years as Mr. McFarland and the Canadian Co-Operative Wheat Producers Limited have been nothing more or less than a board conducting voluntary market operations. A man was entitled to sell or not sell to Mr. McFarland as he saw fit. I submit that so far as the western wheat grower is concerned that the voluntary system should be continued until there has been more opportunity to consider the matter. No; I do not pick days. If the minister really wants to know the truth, I may tell him that I did not speak yesterday because I was not well. That was the only reason. Perhaps I should not be speaking this afternoon. But I want to say that what I have tried to do is correct a statement which the minister made in reply to a statement that I had made that afternoon.
I hear from a good many of the wheat producers in western Canada. My constituency is wholly a wheat-producing constituency. I was over the whole of it last autumn from one end to the other. My constituents at various points-and all of them are wheat farmers-expressed deep resentment at the

Grain
proposal once again to introduce this bank loan plan which-as the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said in the speech he has just made-was proved to be a failure in 1953. We knew that it would be not only unpopular but mainly useless in 1951 when we moved the amendment to which I have referred calling for advances. We are therefore opposing this legislation because we disbelieve in it, because we think it is inadequate and because we think it is resented by the people who sent us here, and we are saying so. Not only are we saying so but at every opportunity we are going to vote against it.
I know we were the only party in the house which voted against it at the resolution stage. We voted against it then because we hoped that if the house showed its disapproval of this legislation at the resolution stage, a bill such as the one we have before us might not be introduced but rather that the government might reconsider its proposals and introduce another bill designed to meet the needs of the western wheat growers. I think that is what they hoped for as well. The government have not seen fit to do so. They have adopted this policy and they are going to put it through, I have no doubt. But they will put it through over our opposition.
Let it not be said that the opposition that has been indicated in this house to this measure is in any way fomented by those who are opposed to the wheat board. That was said on occasion but I am glad to say it has not been said just lately. Let that not be said. The Winnipeg Free Press, the newspaper which has been said to be opposed to the board, was opposed to the board, I know, when the board was originally set up and for some years afterwards. But as I read the Free Press today, even it accepts the situation as an accomplished fact, realizing that the producers want such a method of marketing and realizing perhaps that with an international wheat agreement-which I may say I hope will be consummated-this is the only way in which wheat can be marketed successfully under agreements and on the markets of the world. Hence today I believe there is unanimity in Canada-except for a minority who would like to restore the entire grain business to the grain exchange-in support of the wheat board method of marketing. We therefore do not need to argue that point.
I am going to say this to my hon. friends of the Liberal party. While I have said-and it is my belief-that they were opposed to this method of marketing for a long time, and that they wanted to do all they could to keep the
[Mr. Coldwell.l
voluntary system or, as they call it, the competitive system, because of the experience of the government during the war years and subsequently I believe they, like the rest of us, now believe that the wheat board is here to stay and that it is the best method of marketing.
But that does not mean that, under circumstances such as those which now exist, our farmers are able to market enough grain to pay their expenses and their taxes; and those taxes are an extremely serious consideration in all the three western provinces where wheat is grown in large quantities. The municipalities in Manitoba, in Saskatchewan and in Alberta are all finding it difficult to maintain their essential services and their school systems. These bank loans will not suffice. If a man can get a bank loan under this legislation, he can get a bank loan anyway. If he is marketing some of his wheat, the bank loan he will get is so small that it will make little difference to him and it will not enable him to pay his taxes or to prepare his machinery for seeding in the springtime. So it is that we are opposing this legislation because we should like to have seen something different. Today, of course, I suppose it does not matter, from the point of view of the western farmers, whether or not this legislation is supported by the opposition members. Loans have been made and the guarantee was given by the Minister of Defence Production-

Yes, the guarantee was given by the Minister of Finance to the banks, and I have no doubt that guarantee will be carried out. I want to say this to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), who is also not in his seat: When this was contemplated the proper thing to have done was to have called parliament together to have this legislation, if this was to be the legislation, passed by the house.
I think the pledging of money on behalf of Canada is not a matter that can be done by order in council. If there is one traditional right we have in this House of Commons, it is the control over expenditure. It may be a very shadowy thing in a house where the government has the huge majority it has in this parliament, but the real function of this house it not to initiate legislation, which is the business of the government, but to control expenditures. This might have been a very heavy expenditure. I do not know what amounts are out at the moment but I imagine they are relatively small and yet, in many

people's eyes, probably quite substantial. This has been done without the consent of this parliament.
Parliament should have been called together when the situation was realized last September, and provision made, not for bank loans or loans upon which the farmers would have to pay 5 per cent interest on what has been described in this house as their own earnings. At the same time we were told that a powerful company, controlled in almost every particular in the United States, would have very great advances, not in the form of actual cash but in the form of a great national project which I think should not be alienated, at 3-5 per cent interest. The contrast is striking, Mr. Speaker. So I am rising this afternoon to support the amendment we have moved, just as I rose to support the other amendment we moved, to give this the six months' hoist.

We have listened to this debate for some time, Mr. Speaker, and I was going to say mostly but I will say nearly all the speeches from the opposition were irrelevant or repe-titous. I think, therefore, we on this side of the house have good reason for not intervening in the debate to prolong it uselessly. But having just listened to the speech by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) and the speech by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) I think that one or two remarks would be in order at this time.
In my opinion the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar put his finger on the crux of the problem when he said he is of the opinion that the surplus wheat we have in the west at this time is a great national asset. In saying that, he is repeating what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has already said, that it is no calamity to have a great wheat surplus because at this time they have bad weather conditions in Europe which may lead to a bad crop and we will undoubtedly sell our wheat crop eventually.

What impressed me most in what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, if the hon. member will allow me to continue, was that he thought the people of Canada should pay for the carrying of this surplus wheat; that is the crux of the problem. We on this side think that money should be advanced to the farmers but that they should pay interest on it. The people on the other side think that money should be advanced to the farmers without interest. Who is going to pay the interest? Evidently it is the people of Canada. Is it fair that the people of
Grain
Canada should be called upon to pay interest for the farmers in the west? Why should I not say, as the member for the Madeleine islands, that the people of Canada should pay interest to the fishermen on their fish products that have been canned but not sold or that have been frozen and not sold. There are many other instances. You could go to the coal mines or anything that is produced in the country.
You could say, why should the people of Canada not make advances on all of these things that are produced? Why should they pay interest on such money? I think what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has stated illustrates how weak is the position of the opposition and how strong is the position of the government. He has put his finger right on it. Why should the people of Canada pay that interest for the western farmers if they do not pay interest for all the other producers of this country?
Now, I want to mention what the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said. I am sorry he has left the house. He has a reputation, which I am sure is well deserved, of being a distinguished lawyer. He has made a statement that I think is a legal heresy. His statement was more or less along the same line as that of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. He says the farmers have produced this wheat, and therefore they should be paid for it and they should not have to pay interest on the money they get for it, whether or not the wheat is sold. There again, you cannot support a statement like that if you have a legal brain and if you know what the law is all about. Why should a person be paid for something he has produced before that thing has been sold? Why should he get that money without having to pay interest on it? I think perhaps all the western farmers can expect us to do for them is just what we are doing, to facilitate their getting bank loans on which they pay interest. It is only the normal thing. Why should they get money on their products, without paying interest, without having sold their products?
I think we are doing the right thing for the farmers. I am sure the farmers in the west are just as good citizens as any of us are. I am sure they are pleased with the legislation we are passing for them, which is privileged legislation, but I do not begrudge it. I am sure they realize they are getting a privilege through this legislation. I am sure the members of the opposition, and particularly the members of the C.C.F. group who have carried on a filibuster against this legislation, have not gained one vote but on the contrary have lost votes in the western part of the country.

I wish to say a few words on Bill No. 82, Mr. Speaker. A number of us in this group at the resolution stage criticized the government's proposal at some length. On the other hand, it was a resolution to introduce a bill and we did not vote against the resolution because we wanted to see just what was going to be in the bill. We wanted to be in a position to accept or reject the bill on its merits. After we read the bill, there was no doubt in our minds that the bill should be rejected. Therefore, when the C.C.F. moved an amendment to report the subject matter of this bill to the committee on agriculture, we supported it.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) suggested that such action would kill the bill. However, I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) showed quite clearly that that would not necessarily be the result, but that the subject matter could be sent to the committee on agriculture, and if the committee saw fit it could recommend to the house that the bill be again presented. Then, the bill could be put through the house if the house saw fit. Therefore the argument of the minister was not a very sound one.
However, I did present an alternative to the government. I suggested that after second reading the bill itself should be sent to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. There was nothing unique about the proposal. We do it every year. At the time I was somewhat disappointed, but I will not say surprised, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) rejected the suggestion and said the government was not prepared to send the bill to the committee. I think it is a pity. It is quite an important measure. I should like to see a bill of this kind given far more consideration than it is going to get, and perhaps be extended into something of a permanent character, useful in the future instead of just for the moment. If this bill had been sent to the agriculture committee and we had called representatives from various farm organizations, then they could have given their views on the bill itself.
I do not know whether the government actually consulted any of the officials of the main farm organizations on the drafting of this bill. I doubt very much whether they did because I was speaking to one of the officials of one of the main farm organizations just two days ago, and I asked him what he thought of the bill. He said: "I have never seen it". He has not the slightest idea what is in the bill. He could not say whether he was in favour of it or not until he had seen it.

speechtext: Yes, of course. That is the reason. The reason they have not asked for loans is that they do not want to pay interest. They are hoping to be able to sell the wheat. That is the reply to the hon. member who just rose to his feet. The reason the farmers should not have to pay interest is this. The government is in control of the marketing of wheat and of transportation. Last year sales broke down. They could not get orders. This year they could get orders but they could not get box cars. It is transportation that has broken down. The government is in full charge of that policy. The farmers have a right to expect the government to at least pay them the price of the normal delivery for wheat on the farm. That is all they are asking for, the normal delivery of wheat. speechtext:
That shows just how little the hon. member knows. The minister himself said that some points have a one-bushel quota. Is that a normal crop? Some points have a 2-bushel quota, and some have a 3-bushel quota. Does the hon. member call that an average crop? It might be in his part of the country, but if so, he must live on a stone pile. That is certainly not the situation in western Canada where the average yield even in an average year was around 17 bushels. In the past five years the average yield has been considerably in excess of that amount.
While I say there is a 1-bushel quota at some points, there are many farmers at those points who have not been able to deliver one bushel on the 1-bushel quota. Most points have been able to deliver the initial amount of 300 bushels, but there are many farmers who have not been able to deliver one bushel on the 1-bushel quota. It is not very pleasant for those farmers when they see a point 30 miles away where the farmers can sell three bushels to the acre and they are unable to sell one. As a result of that situation they

Grain
have bills in town at the different stores unpaid. They would like to pay them. They are not paying any interest on those bills. Can you blame them for not going to borrow money and pay interest on it in order to pay another bill upon which they are not paying any interest? It would not be very good business; it might be good ethics. That is why many farmers are taking loans today to pay bills on which they do not have to pay any interest. They are doing that because they like to pay their debts. They would rather pay interest on the debt to the hanks than continue to allow the bill to run in the store, because they realize it is a hardship on the storekeeper. I would say that is true of 95 per cent of the cases. It just goes to prove that the farmers of the west, as a rule, are honest men and like to pay their debts. But they think there should be a limit to the extent to which they should be plunged steadily further and further into debt. They have the right to expect that they should be able to deliver a normal delivery. All that the farmers in the constituency that I represent ask for is for the government to make an advance up to 50 per cent of the normal delivery. By advance in that case they meant payment on the wheat and not a loan. They rejected the idea of a loan. They suggested that the normal delivery should be on the basis of 8 bushels to the acre because they were afraid that if it stated merely the normal delivery the government might take only 2 or 3 bushels to the acre. That is the stand they have taken to date. I have absolutely no hesitation in saying that if they read this bill they will reject it.
The farmers did not tell me that. As a matter of fact when matters of this kind come before a convention in my constituency and I try to get the farmers to give me a directive as to whether I should vote for or against something, they have always insisted that I use my best judgment. They say, "You are on the spot; you know the facts; therefore we are going to leave it to your discretion to decide whether you vote for or against the measure." I am using my discretion at the present time in rejecting this bill. The title of the bill reads:
An act to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain.
I suppose that could be said to be the purpose of the bill. I would appreciate the minister correcting me if I am wrong, but I gathered from what he said that the purpose of the bill is to make loans available to the weaker farmer, the small farmer, the new farmer or the farmer who is financially embarrassed. I take it that is the main purpose

of the bill, that is the class he has in view. I think he will agree that this is a fair interpretation of his attitude. I do not wish to misinterpret him and it would take too long to find his actual statement by going through all the pages of Hansard. I take it that this is the general purpose.
Therefore the minister will agree that if that is the purpose it is most important that this bill should carry out that purpose. I claim that the bill does not carry out that purpose. As a matter of fact, I claim that many farmers who might borrow under this bill will be worse off than farmers who borrow from other sources. I will give the reason why I say I think it will actually worsen their position. My contention is that the contents of this bill violate the purposes of the bill. We have heard it said that some members are dirt farmers, that some have had no farming experience. Speaking personally, I think I am in as good a position as anyone to speak on this bill.

I am not supporting or rejecting this bill on the basis of what I need, I am supporting or rejecting it on the basis of what I feel the people in the area I represent need. I have farmed for some 40 years. Let me state frankly that 75 per cent of that time I was short of capital. I have had lots of experience in borrowing from banks, so I know something about this situation. It is true that for the last 25 per cent of the time I probably did not need to, but for the first 75 per cent I did.
I homesteaded in the west in 1909. I did not have any capital, I did not have any money at all. I used to work in railway construction camps for a few months in the summer in order to get enough money to run my farm.

speechtext:
By 1914 I had just started to get on my feet, and then I was overseas for five years. When I came back I had to start all over again. Everything I had was worn out, my machinery was all worn out and the price of everything was sky high. I settled under the Soldier Settlement Act which was a pretty tough act, quite different from the present Veterans' Land Act. Within a few

years the value of my chattels had fallen to about half their original value. It was about 1929 before I again started to get on my feet.
In 1929 I was still farming with horses. I realized then, as did most farmers, that if I was going to make any real progress I would have to have a mechanized farm. I went to the bank and asked for a loan in order to buy a tractor. I was quite interested in the attitude taken by the bank manager. He had my financial statement and he told me I was in excellent shape, that in a short time I would be sitting on top of the world, but he then went on to give me some sound advice. He told me not to borrow any money with which to buy a tractor because within a short period of time we would be going into a depression.
That was in 1929. I have always wondered why a bank manager was able to tell me in 1929-it was not being publicized in the press -that we were going into a depression when credit would be restricted and therefore it would be unwise for me to buy a tractor. I continued along with my horses. Just two years later I went to the bank again, but I could not borrow a cent although my physical assets were exactly the same or a little bit better than in 1929. In 1929 I could have borrowed enough on my personal note to buy a tractor, but in 1931 I could not borrow a cent.
I might mention that they had changed the bank manager in the meantime. Any time they bring in a new policy of restricting loans they seem to change their managers, because it might embarrass a bank manager to refuse a loan to an old friend. I thought it very strange that with no change in physical assets I could not borrow any money.
We all remember the depression, and I am not going to deal with it. We got through it. I did not go under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act because I did not like it, just as I do not like this bill. There were too many restrictions in it. However, we farmers got through the depression and then came some good times. I admit quite frankly that we have had some good times.
There are many farmers who realized that in order to produce efficiently they had to have an efficient unit. Professor Hope has defined an efficient unit as two sections of moderate land or one section of heavy land. The area which I represent is a good one, and many farmers thought it advisable to expand their land holdings and borrowed money with which to buy land. They borrowed money to buy farm machinery under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
Those are the farmers who are in so much difficulty today. They are not new farmers,

they are not young farmers, they are not small farmers; they are fairly large farmers. They have been farming quite a long time and have lots of experience. But they have incurred heavy liabilities which normally would be met from their sales of wheat. These are the farmers who are facing a great deal of difficulty.

You want to know whether I think the eastern farmer should be prepared to pay income tax for the purpose of helping to pay interest or to make loans available without interest? There need not be any interest involved, because the government could make advances to the farmers and get the money from its own institution, the Bank of Canada, without borrowing from the chartered banks. But it goes far beyond that. Even if it was costing some money I say that the western farmers are entitled to it because during the latter part of the war they subsidized the consumers of Canada to the tune of around $136 million. The same thing applies to other products of the farm.
Therefore a suggestion like that does not embarrass me at all. The hon. member talks about income tax. Let me remind him that the majority of the income taxes paid by farmers is paid by farmers in the west and not by farmers in the east. I suggest it would be a good idea if the Minister of National Revenue sent as many inspectors into that part of the country as to the west; then they would collect a little more money. The only reason they collect more income tax in the west is the fact that wheat is one of the main products and it is very easy for the Department of National Revenue to check on the farmers' incomes. In the east, where the farmers peddle their products in the local markets, there is no check at all, and I think many of them get away with murder.
