speechtext:
I am sorry the minister went away, though the parliamentary assistant is here, because I do not like to say anything specifically referring to the minister when he is out. I was just going to say that I have been puzzled at times' during this debate over the fact that the minister seems to display

Grain
quite an ignorance of the true situation in regard to agriculture. However, that is perhaps only natural, because he is not a farmer and the problems are quite complex.
I believe he thinks he is stating the facts when he makes certain statements, but when I spoke the last time he made two or three interjections, and I was somewhat amazed at the questions he asked. I should have thought he must have known at that time that his questions did not really make sense, as for instance when he suggested that no large farmer had trouble getting money from the banks.
I have just explained why so many farmers are having trouble. It is because many of the big farmers have borrowed to expand their capital in the form of machinery, and have borrowed to expand their land holdings. They are large farmers, but they are heavily in debt. They may have 20,000 or 30,000 bushels of wheat on the farm but cannot sell it. If they could sell their wheat they would be able to meet their obligations. They cannot borrow money from the bank because they have gone as far as they can go in that direction. They are not interested in legislation like this. They are interested in being able to sell their wheat.
Right through this debate the minister has shown that he does not understand the situation as between the smaller farmer and the larger farmer. He jumped to the conclusion that the large farmer must be considerably better off than a small farmer. I agree that the size of the farm is a great factor, but there is another factor even greater, and that is the quality of the soil. You could have a three-section unit of marginal land which would not be nearly as good as a one-section unit in, for instance, gumbo land.
The constituency I represent is remarkable for the different types of soil it contains. On the western side of the constituency we have the gumbo plain, probably the best wheat country in Canada. I resided on the edge of that area. This legislation will be of little if any value to the farmers in that area. Whatever money they want to borrow, they can borrow from the banks. But they do not want to borrow today because, as I say, they do not like paying interest. They are already paying enough interest on their land holdings, machinery and so on. As they have the wheat, they feel they should be able to sell it and so pay off their obligations. If they want to borrow from the banks, they can borrow without this legislation.
Then we have the northern area of my constituency, around Stettler on the C.P.R. line. That is not such good land, but there is a greater rainfall there. I think the same
fMr. Quelch.l
thing applies to that area as to the western part of the constituency; it is a mixed farming area. Then you have an entirely different situation on the eastern side of the constituency. From Hanna east is what used to be known as the drought area of Alberta. This is where irrigation would be put in if the Red Deer diversion scheme were proceeded with. The government has been talking about that and making surveys for it since 1922, but the only time there is any real activity is just before an election, and I suppose next June there will be a great deal of activity there again. The farmers are still hopeful, however, that some day that program will be put into effect.
That is a dry area. Back in the years around 1919 or 1920 most of that land was sold for tax arrears. Most of the farmers got hopelessly into debt and the land was put up for sale. The mortgage companies did not consider the land worth sufficient to pay the reserve bid and so the land reverted to the provincial government. The provincial government realized that no farmer could make a living in that area on a half-section unit. Most of the land was taken back, and then any farmer who had a quarter or half section in that area was allowed to lease from the government about 2,000 acres. The units in that area are about 2,000 acres per farmer. They had to own one-quarter sections.
Just because a farm is large it does not mean that the farmer is in a position where he can borrow all the money he needs. As a matter of fact, the farmers in that area-all those big farmers-until recently, at least, were never able to go to the banks and borrow much money. Indeed, that area was blacklisted, and the farm loan board refused to make loans in that area. I have received many protests and have taken them up with the farm loan board, which has insisted it has not blacklisted the area but has judged each application on its merits and found the situation does not warrant making loans in that area.
However, in the past four or five years we have had heavy rains in that area and, generally speaking, there have been good crops for the past five years and these farmers are getting on their feet. Four or five years ago the average yield in that area was only six or seven bushels to the acre. During the last few years it has been about 16 or 17 bushels to the acre.
I want to relate that situation to this bill, because there you have large farms with fair yields of wheat, about 16 bushels to the acre. Take a farmer in that area getting a loan under this proposal. I do not say he would

not get a loan. He might get a loan of $1,500. What is the situation in which he finds himself if he takes a loan under this bill? We shall say, for example, that a two-bushel quota is put into effect and that the farmer has six or seven hundred acres of cultivated land, which would be a very moderate holding in that area. Many of the units are 2,000 acres, because it is considered necessary for a farmer to have that amount of land to make a living. At one time a farmer there was allowed to carry only three head of livestock on a quarter section, but that has been changed a little owing to the rains in recent years.
When a two-bushel quota is put into effect, that farmer takes a load of wheat to the elevator agent and asks what grade he can get. Probably there will be a dispute between him and the elevator agent, and the agent may say it is 4 while the farmer will say, "It is a good 3, and I am not going to take 4." What can the farmer do in a case like that, unless he is prepared to sell it for what the agent says he will pay? He will have to put that wheat into storage and a sample will be sent to the head office. Then the grade is sent back, and he is paid on that grade.
However, under this act he is not allowed to put that wheat into storage. Therefore, any farmer who has borrowed under this legislation, and who in order to get a fair grade tries to put his wheat into storage until such time as a grade has been arranged, puts the elevator agent in the position where he can be prosecuted if he allows the grain to be stored.

I am certainly glad to hear that, because that was one of my very strong objections to the bill. Then there is another objection. The minister will probably say this one is not quite so well founded. He will probably say the provision is necessary, but I can tell the minister that it is going to be bitterly resented.
Take two farmers who are living side by side. I am speaking from experience in this case; it is something that has happened many times. Two farmers are living side by side and one is hailed out 100 per cent. What happens in a case like that? If his neighbour
Grain
has a good crop the practice in the past has often been for the farmer with the good crop to lend his neighbour who has been hailed out maybe a thousand bushels of oats, barley or wheat. I have done it myself, and I have had grain lent me.
The farmer who gets the grain and has no money can deliver the wheat on his own quota and sell it. Sometimes he makes a dicker with the farmer from whom he got the wheat and pays some of the money to him. If any farmer does that under this legislation he can be fined $500 and, if the hon. member for Prince Albert is right, he can land in jail. If the farmers find that out they will be hopping mad, because it is very often the only way they can help themselves.
I think the minister will agree that is a fine co-operative spirit, and nothing in this legislation should allow that fine co-operative spirit to be destroyed. The farmers help themselves.
I do not believe that anywhere in Canada you will find a better co-operative spirit that you will find amongst the farmers of the west. If one gets in bad shape his neighbours help him out if they can.

Well, the minister sees one ship and he talks about a fleet. I am not suggesting that at all. Remember that the farmer can only get a loan of up to 50 per cent of the amount of wheat. The minister knows that in many cases the farmer will have far more than the amount of wheat needed to cover the loan. Therefore it should be possible in a case like that for the farmer to transfer some of that wheat to a neighbour if he so desires.
Under the legislation he pledges so much of that wheat. He tells the bank manager how much wheat he can deliver and the price he expects to get, but so long as he states a certain amount of wheat and a price and the bank manager agrees to that, then any wheat the farmer holds in excess of that amount should be his property to do what he likes with. If he wants to lend a thousand bushels to his neighbour who has been hailed out there should not be any danger of that man being prosecuted or thrown in jail. At least the legislation should be wide enough to allow a certain amount of discretion so that the farmer can discuss the matter with the bank or with the wheat board and get permission for that transaction.
The minister knows that the situation today is difficult. We will not talk about who is to blame for the situation, but we are faced with

a situation today and it is a difficult one. Therefore anything the farmers can do among themselves to try to relieve the situation, to try to relieve the pressure, is something the minister should be glad to help them to do. I hope the minister can say the same thing about that provision as he said about the other one, that an amendment will be moved to modify its operation.

the stand taken by some of the people representing organizations at that conference. Anyone who wants to check this can see the record in the hands of Mrs. Norman because as the conference went on she kept notes of what everybody said.
When this matter came before the conference on the afternoon of September 27, 1955, one of the first speakers was Mr. Wesson, who first of all dealt with the statistical position and gave various statistics. This is Mrs. Norman's record of what he said:
The shortage of cash was the problem. Wheat pool opposes advances of wheat board through elevators. Mr. Schulz continued debate on Mr. Wesson's proposal. He stated he was in favour of Mr. Wesson's proposal but suggested that the government should absorb all interest.

If these hon. gentlemen want to chip in every few minutes with interruptions while I am speaking, I may tell them there is still plenty of time left for them to speak.
As I said at the outset, I rose to comment particularly on the contribution that the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine made to this debate. During his speech he made a couple of rather astounding statements. He asked the question, and he repeated it later when he interrupted the hon. member for Acadia, why should the farmers be paid for what they have produced and what has not yet been sold? That question in itself indicates a lack of understanding of this whole issue. I hope the hon. member is not speaking on behalf of the farmers of eastern Canada. Certainly if he is, he is doing a tremendous amount of harm to their cause.
In the first place no one in this house has asked that the grain producers generally be paid for all their production. The farmers themselves have not asked for that. They have asked for an advance of approximately half of what they expect normally to deliver, and that is a long way from what they have produced, as the figures are there to prove. The question indicates the hon. member does not understand the permit book. He does not understand the quota system. He does not understand that farmers are not asking, nor are the representatives of the farmers, that they be paid cash for all the grain they have produced, even though that is what is being done in the United States. We have heard time and again from the members on the other side that the farmers in Canada are being very well treated in comparison with the farmers in other countries. But if the government applied the same method that is being applied in the United States, then they would pay the farmer for all his production and in addition to that would pay him for storing the grain on his farm.
All the farmers are asking, and all we in this group are asking, is a long way from that. We are asking that they be given the opportunity to obtain an advance on a portion of
the quota that they are able to deliver under the present set-up. That is an entirely different thing from the interpretation the hon. member gave to it. But let us follow that a step further. If this parliament were to accept, heaven forbid, the philosophy that farmers should not be paid for what they have produced until it is sold, where does that leave our whole Agricultural Prices Support Act? Where does it leave the support price under butter and the support price under eggs? Where does it leave all these support prices which have been accepted as part and parcel of the agriculture policy? If the government, in a moment of weakness, were to give in to the advice of the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine it would mean the complete destruction of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. He is doing a distinct disservice to every dairy producer, every producer of eggs, not only in western Canada but in his own constituency. I think on reflection the hon. member would want to withdraw that statement and apologize for having made it.
He goes on to say that this bill is a privilege. He wonders why the farmers are dissatisfied with the present bill because it is a privilege. This privilege is an opportunity for the farmer to go further into debt, an opportunity to pay interest on money that is properly coming to him. I am not at liberty to refer to the clauses in the bill, but it is well known that one of the privileges in it is that if a farmer should happen to misunderstand one of the multifarious forms that have been drawn up, forms that were drawn up before this bill has passed, he can be fined $500. In addition to that penalty he would have to pay the amount of money still owing on his loan. I suppose that in default of paying his fine he could be imprisoned; that is the kind of privilege that is being offered under this bill.

At no time have I or any member of this group claimed that it does not help the western farmer. If it is of any assistance in the selling of feed grain then, of course, to that extent it is of some assistance to agriculture generally. But the point is, it is a direct subsidy to those who feed that grain in eastern Canada. Yet there are hon. members from eastern Canada who rise in their places and-I have no doubt without consulting the farmers at all-they take the stand that they are their farmers and they speak for them without consulting their opinions at all. They say that their farmers are objecting to something that may be of advantage to the grain producers who are willing to pay their share of freight assistance to ship the feed grain to eastern Canada.
All we are asking is that the members from eastern Canada take a fair and reasonable stand on this question. I think if they would only stop to think they would realize that in many ways the people of western Canada have been instrumental ever since confederation in subsidizing to a very great extent the people of eastern Canada in the form of tariff duties, for example. Every day that goes by hundreds of thousands of dollars are paid out by the people of western Canada to help to protect industry in eastern Canada. If they would stop to think of that I am sure they would take a little more reasonable attitude than they are taking on this question.
However, the question that is before us is whether this bill should be read a second time. We have stated, I believe in clear and unmistakable terms, that we are not prepared to support the bill on second reading. The other opposition parties have also indicated now that they will not accept the bill on second reading. We are basing our stand not only on what is contained in the bill, bad as it is, but also on the opinions as they were expressed in convention by the major farm organizations in western Canada.
Regardless of what the hon. member for Rosthern may say, regardless of how he tries to twist around what happened at the Saskatoon conference, regardless of what other members of the Liberal party may try to say, if they were to go out to western Canada today and test public opinion on this question I am sure they would come back quite convinced that this bill is not the answer to the problem. What is more, they would come back convinced that they are making a major mistake by assuming that just because at one time or another one, two or three of the leaders of some of the farm organizations made certain statements which make it appear as though they are supporting the bank loans, they were in fact speaking for the farmers

of that organization, because subsequent events proved that that was not so.
If the government feel so stubborn about this question, if they feel so sure of their position, I for one am prepared to let them test public opinion on this issue. Let them call an election tomorrow and actually find out the feelings of western Canada on this question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious from the nature of the discussion taking place on this bill today that we are dealing with a very complex problem that has a very serious impact on the general economy of Canada, and more particularly on the whole economy of the prairies. I am taking advantage of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) to lend my support to the suggestion that this particular piece of legislation be given the six months' hoist. I do so because I have considered the matter quite seriously as it would affect my own area, and I can quite readily come to the conclusion that nothing would be lost, so far as assisting the critical cash shortage among the farm population of my particular constituency is concerned if this legislation is never passed.
The last time I contributed to the discussion I emphasized why the bill is not wanted by the farmers of my area, and why if passed it will do nothing to solve the basic problem. The hon. member for Rosthern has been recapitulating certain arguments that have been made in the house. I would like to suggest, in refutation, an up to date point of view representing a cross section of the prairie farm population, a point of view, as a matter of fact, which was expressed to the government no later than yesterday, February 16. The interprovineial farm union, council delegation appeared before the government at that time, as they have appeared before other groups in this house, and repeated in no uncertain terms, verbally as well as in their written statement, that they favour the cash advance principle rather than the legislation that we have before us today.
We have had contributions from members from other parts of the country as well as from western Canada. As I have listened to the contributions from members from eastern Canada, I have been amazed. Some of those contributions have been formal speeches; others have been interjections. I have been amazed, Mr. Speaker, at the lack of understanding of the difficulty with which the farm population, the wheat grower especially, is faced at the moment. I refer particularly to the interjection of the hon. member for the Iles-de-la-Madeleine and others
Grain
who interjected, who feel that the legislation before us is in the form of a subsidy to the grain growers on the prairies.
I endeavoured to point out the other day that at no time has the prairie farmer ever been subsidized by any part of the Canadian economy. There is the misunderstanding that the operations of the Canadian wheat board involve a form of subsidy. But, as I emphasized the other day-and 1 repeat it this afternoon because the point does not seem to have penetrated-the farmer has paid out of the returns received from the marketing operations of the wheat board for every penny that he received. He has never been subsidized by the federal treasury. And of course the bill we have before us places him in the same independent position.
The point we are making is that the principle enunciated in the bill does not begin to meet the situation in which the farmer finds himself at the moment. It would seem that not only is there failure on the part of members from other sections of Canada who have intervened in the debate to understand the nature of the problem, but it would appear that the administration itself, the ministers most concerned, also fail to appreciate fully the nature of the problem.
I am going to deal with only one phrase in the bill which tends to emphasize the point I have just made. The bill refers to the cash shortage problem as a temporary financial difficulty. One reason I have opposed the legislation is that I feel this is not a temporary situation. If it were a temporary and passing situation no doubt the piece of legislation we have before us today would suffice, but it becomes increasingly obvious with the passing of time that the farmer himself regards the bill as quite ineffective to meet the problem. Certainly the fact that the government have described the bill as meeting a temporary situation indicates that they are almost completely unaware of the real nature of the problem.
Actually there has always been a shortage of cash among the farmers of western Canada. Until 1930 the farmers there operated largely under a subsistence economy. They did not have much to do with the exchange of money in any shape or form. They were suspicious of banks and the whole monetary scheme of things. I think this fact is dramatically demonstrated in the new forms of political expression which have emerged in western Canada. All of them have had as a basic part of their ideology some emphasis on the suspicious attitude toward the existing financial system. Farmers had got themselves into a situation of debt during the thirties, and that only increased their anxiety.

Grain
More recently because of changing circumstances the farmer has been moving toward a cash economy. Whereas he had been able to get along reasonably successfully on a subsistence basis, living as far as possible from the production of his own farm, today he is dependent upon money whether he likes it or not. He must have ready cash in order to meet current operations of his farming business. This is not a new situation, it is merely something which has come to a head because of the rapidly changing circumstances since the war, particularly in the past three or four years. It seems obvious that the government has failed to appreciate the nature of this problem.
One reason the situation has become critical from the standpoint of the Canadian farmer is the changing agricultural situation in our neighbour to the south. If we fully appreciated the change in the production and marketing of wheat we would readily come to the conclusion that we are faced with more than a temporary financial situation. Statistics are available so that he who runs may read. For example, we see that today the United States is producing annually more than 1,000 million bushels of wheat, whereas before the war it produced on the average some 700 million bushels of wheat. We must appreciate the difficulty facing the Canadian wheat economy because of that changed situation.
The consumption of wheat remains pretty well static. It is a well known fact that the demand for wheat remains practically stationary regardless of the level of production. When there is an increased level of production the demand remains almost static. The total world demand for wheat has grown ?ery slightly in relation to the total increase in world population. Domestic consumption in the United States has remained fairly static; therefore they have had to turn to the export market. Ever since the Canadian west was settled the export market traditionally has been largely taken care of by the wheat producers of the Canadian prairies. During the 10-year period 1930-39 the United States producers exported 59-9 million bushels, whereas for the comparative 10-year period 1946-55 they exported 309-3 million bushels. Such an increase would tend to suggest that somebody is going to suffer in the markets of the world and unfortunately that somebody has been the western Canada wheat producer.
It is equally obvious that the United States is going to remain a sharp competitor of the prairie grain producer, so that the cash shortage referred to as a temporary financial shortage is not going to decrease within the

foreseeable future. Actually Canadian exports have decreased proportionately in the past three years. We maintained our position fairly well up until the end of the war in Korea, but since that time Canada has been occupying a declining position in the export markets of the world. That problem has been intensified by the fact that there has been no real positive action on the part of the government to improve our exports.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a brief word about this case. First of all, since we so often draw attention to the cases in which paid investigators or professional detectives are used as witnesses, I should be fair and point out that in 'this case no detectives or investigators were employed. The witnesses who appeared, on behalf of the plaintiff seemed to be people who had never appeared before in a case such as this. But after reading this case I am also impressed with the tragedy of the

situation. I note in particular that there are two children, one 8 years of age and one 3 years of age.
Having read this case, it does seem to me it is the type of case where some other recourse might have been had, where counselling of some kind might have been effective. Because of that I feel unhappy about parliament granting this divorce in the very easy manner in which it seems to go through, particularly through this House of Commons.

subtopic: HAZEL LORETTA NOSEWORTHY JOHNSTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a rather unusual bill. In the

Private Bills'-Divorce
petition it is stated that the petitioner resides in the town of North Sydney, but when the case came before the subcommittee on January 17 it appeared that the petitioner resided in Montreal. The evidence does not make it quite clear how it is that in the one place it is stated that she resides in North Sydney and in the other place in Montreal. My learned friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre informs me that while this couple, when they were married and after they were married, resided in North Sydney, because the husband deserted and returned to Montreal his wife automatically became domiciled in the province of Quebec. This unfortunate woman has a tragic story as told in the Senate, and is put to the expense of coming to Ottawa to present her case.
There is another unusual feature in this case. The co-respondent appeared and gave evidence. It is obvious that this family has been broken and of course the customary questions were asked and answered with respect to whether or not there was any collusion. I think this is the first case of this particular type which I happen to have noticed this year, where the co-respondent has come before the committee, admitted the charges and a divorce has been granted.
When this case comes before the house committee I think there should be some discussion with respect to the information given in the petition as to the residence of this woman and the information given in the minutes of the subcommittee of January 14 setting forth that the woman is domiciled in the province of Quebec. The question should be cleared up whether a woman who has always lived in Nova Scotia and is deserted by her husband who goes to the province of Quebec should be put to the expense of coming to Ottawa to seek a divorce.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is another bill where the principal witness is the co-respondent. Once again, as with some of the others to which I have referred today, having read the bill it seems to me we simply do not know whether or not this is a divorce that should be granted. The more I read bills of this kind, and there are a lot more like them before us today, the more I feel we
1326	HOUSE OF
Private Bills-Divorce simply are not competent'as a group of members, with all the other business we have, to be dealing with cases of this kind.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: I am glad to hear you say "order", Mr. Speaker. I think the whole business is out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: I fully agree with the hon. member. As a matter of fact, I have been looking up some of the authorities and want to submit some observations to him. The hon. member concluded his remarks a moment ago by saying that he does not think members are competent to deal with these matters. No doubt he was referring to a bill he introduced the other day which will eventually come before the house, namely his proposal to refer this whole business, as he calls it, to the exchequer court. That measure will come up and he will have ample opportunity at that time to put forward the suggestion contained in that bill. Therefore the suggestion should not be anticipated in the discussion of this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: With respect, I did not suggest it. You may be reading my mind, but I did not say it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext:
The hon. member almost said it without referring to the bill. I have heard him make remarks before with respect to this whole business and he will perhaps permit me to keep in my mind some of the words he does say in the house from time to time.
I want to refer particularly to the procedure that has been followed since five o'clock. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) have spoken to the second reading of some of the divorce bills that have been before the house today. In each of the cases on which they have spoken they have referred to the evidence taken in the Senate. I think they have both referred to members of the Senate who are members of that committee and who acted on it. I have in mind, in looking over these proceedings, that if we are to refer to the actions taken or the opinions expressed by the members of the other house, perhaps we are alluding to proceedings in the other house. That is something which is not allowed in this house. I would refer hon. members to citation 243:
Allusion to debates in the other house are out of order, and there are few orders more important than this for the conduct of debate and for observing courtesy between houses.
There was nothing derogatory in what was said about the members of the other place. As a matter of fact I think it was complimentary. 

Nevertheless I do not believe that in this house we should summarize the work that is being done by one or two individual senators in whatever work they are called upon to perform in the other house. Today, in view of the fact that the comments have not been derogatory, one might say, "Let it go". But tomorrow they may be derogatory and then I would be obliged to stop hon. members from referring to our colleagues in the Senate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: Will Your Honour permit a question?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: I do not rise to argue the point just now but would Your Honour regard what goes on in a committee or in a subcommittee of the other place as coming under the same ban that is stipulated in citation 243 which refers to the other house? The documents from which we have been reading are reports of proceedings in committees and subcommittees. They are not reports of what went on in the other house itself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext:
The hon. member could also have asked whether it relates to debates. The citation to which I have referred, namely citation 243, refers to debates whereas the evidence that has been commented upon constitutes the proceedings in a working committee of the Senate.
Citation 243, although it refers only to "allusion to debates" is only one citation that points out the courtesy which must exist between the two houses. Generally speaking, I think there can be found other citations which are to the effect that in our own house in debate we should refrain from referring to individual members of the other place and what they have done, in whatever capacity, as far as their parliamentary work is concerned.
But there is this further point that I should like to submit to hon. members, namely the very nature of a private bill. When the second reading of a private bill has been given, its principle is to be accepted only conditionally. It is accepted conditionally upon the facts being proven before our own committee to which the bill must be referred. By our own standing orders we provide that, with respect to any private bill, the principle of it is accepted upon condition that it will be referred-we have no choice in the matter-to a standing committee where the facts relating to that bill will be proven. If the preamble is not proven, the bill does not go any further. But if it is proven, it comes back here.
I think the discussion of the evidence taken in the Senate is a premature discussion.

Private Bills-Divorce
Furthermore, to expect that hon. members, in debating the second reading of these bills, will make up their minds only upon the evidence taken in the Senate I think is prejudging what their attitude may be after they have looked at that bill in their own committee.
We know what the practice is and what it has been, but I am now talking about the theory of the whole thing. I am not assuming that our committee, let us say, will not meet -to take an absurd case-to consider these things or, even if they did meet, that they would not pass on them quickly because, let us say, they have confidence in what has taken place on the Senate side. At this moment this bill is to be referred to one of our standing committees. If hon. members wish to do so, they can call all the witnesses -including detectives when there were any- take their own evidence and make up their own minds.
Then in committee of the whole they can review the proceedings that have been reported from our standing committee. But at this moment, in discussing the principle of this bill on second reading, to summarize for the benefit of hon. members who perhaps, like myself, have not read the evidence, while at times it is extremely interesting and entertaining, I think it is something that does not meet the conditions that our rules prescribe.
I am not making a ruling today. I just want to submit these points for the consideration of hon. members. There is no question that, according to citations 769, 770 and 771, on second reading the principle of a private bill is accepted only conditionally. I read now from citation 769:
. . . but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.
The allegations of fact contained in this bill, as far as our own house is concerned, have not been proven. The allegations of fact in the petition have been proved to the satisfaction of the Senate before their committee, and they passed the bill and sent it to this house. But as far as we are concerned, we look at the second reading of this bill only conditionally, notwithstanding what the evidence might have been in the Senate. As far as we are concerned, the facts in connection with this bill have not been proven as far as our own committee is concerned.
Otherwise what would be the reason for sending these bills to our standing committee? You might as well have them dealt with
immediately-I am speaking of the bills to which hon. members have referred tonight- if they opposed them only on the basis of the Senate evidence but did not seek to do anything further in order to defeat them, such as provoking a division or anything like that. What is the purpose of sending them to our own standing committee? Why should they not go from here directly to the committee of the whole and be passed upon immediately? I consider that we are perhaps not adhering to procedure as strictly as we should in considering these private bills.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext:
May I say a word, Mr. Speaker, because I agree with Your Honour that perhaps the procedure we follow might be considered carefully. As a matter of fact, when I was thinking of what I would say if Your Honour gave me the floor for a moment, I was going to start off by agreeing with what you had said about second reading of a private bill being different from second reading of a public bill. In support of my agreement with Your Honour I intended to read the very sentence or two that you have just read from citation 769 of Beauchesne's third edition. Perhaps I might read the same sentence or two again:
A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.
However, Mr. Speaker, as I think you will readily realize, it was my intention not to stop there, as did Your Honour. I intended to go on and read the next sentence or two, which are as follows:
Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the house will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee.
This is the first occasion on which the bill is before the house otherwise than pro forma or in connection with the standing orders; and if the bill be opposed, upon its principle, it is the proper time for attempting its defeat.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I contend that if I, as one of the few members who may happen to have read some of these cases, feel that the principle of a particular bill, the principle of granting a particular divorce as between Mr. and Mrs. A., is objectionable and should not be agreed to, I am within my rights and within the rules of the house in speaking to that bill at second reading. Certainly I would be within my rights in attempting its defeat if I felt that such a bill should not be allowed to pass.	:

Private Bills-Divorce
I hope I was not mistaken if I detected in what Your Honour was saying-Your Honour was reading my mind so perhaps I can read Your Honour's-that Your Honour was almost challenging us to divide the house on some of these bills. Well, in the past we have tried and we have found, to our surprise, cases which we thought should be defeated, and knowing the views of many members in this house on divorce we thought would be defeated, which nevertheless were carried. Whether or not we seek to divide the house I suppose depends upon whether we think, having in mind the circumstances of a particular bill, we can win the majority of the members to our view that a particular bill should be defeated.
Nevertheless, because there are some divorces we think should not be granted, we believe we have the right to draw attention to the ones which in our view are slightly objectionable as we go along so that when we get to ones that are really objectionable we will be in a position to give the house an opportunity to divide on them.
As I say, I agree with Your Honour's contention that these bills are different from public bills. But there is a difference within the difference. As I have pointed out by referring to citation 769, where we think there are objections to a particular divorce, it seems to me that we have the right to discuss it on second reading. Nevertheless, I agree that the whole procedure might be reviewed. We would be glad to discuss it privately with Your Honour or in a committee. Indeed, as Your Honour knows, I would be glad to find some way whereby parliament might get rid of the whole business.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext:
I am sorry if the hon. member detected in anything I have said a view that he could not discuss this bill on second reading. Of course if he feels the principle is objectionable, he will discuss it, and he should discuss it. Under the rules he will be quite in order. But in discussing the principle of this bill I consider that he does not necessarily have to refer to the evidence which has been taken on the Senate side. That is my point.
Suppose the bill were introduced in this house. When second reading was being considered in the Senate they would have no evidence whatever. They accept the principle conditional upon their committee proving the allegations of fact. We are in the same position here. I think if you take for granted that our objection to the bill should be based on the evidence taken in the other place, you do not attach very much importance to the ability of our own committee to prove the facts themselves.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext:
May I point out that in the case of a private bill coming before this house initially, other than a divorce bill, the same general rules apply. We expect the sponsor of such a bill to make an initial statement as to what is involved in that bill. I would be satisfied with the same practice in respect of these bills. If instead of our being given the evidence as a means of finding out something about them, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter) or the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) who is sponsoring some of these bills on his behalf, would speak on second reading and tell us why he thinks we should submit this bill to the committee, as is done in the case of private bills, then I would say that would obviate the necessity of our looking at the evidence furnished to us.
I would be interested in what Your Honour has in mind when you say that a reference to the evidence is not necessarily desirable on second reading. I take it there is no question as to our right to refer to it if we wish. My point is that we are accepting this evidence as something that is given to us in lieu of a statement in support of the bill being made by the mover of second reading.

subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: I wonder if I might make a comment on this. I would support what you have said, Mr. Speaker. I just point out to you that if the evidence is going to be allowed on second reading, and if we consider every bill that has been offered to the house at this time, it would take every hon. member 26J hours to read the evidence. He must be in the same position as my hon. friend to be able to debate a particular bill, and I do not think any hon. member, on this side of the house at least, has 26J hours to spend reading evidence on divorce bills.

subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: I should like to draw to your attention the fact that during the last parliament when a divorce bill was brought before this house, a member on the government side objected to it being proceeded with because members had not received a copy of the evidence. Mr. Speaker upheld that objection at that time because members had not received a copy of the evidence and were therefore not in a position to proceed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: Does the hon. member have the precise date of that incident?

subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: No, I have not, but I know I am speaking correctly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext:
I recall one, and in discussing this point with my predecessor he had doubts as to whether or not hon. members would

have the right to hold up a bill which comes up for second reading only on the ground that the evidence had not been received from the Senate. I think in this case one wants to accommodate all hon. members. I do not think I would, myself, care to have to render a judgment on that point, although I think if I were pressed I would do so. The Clerk informs me that the evidence is always received with the bill, so there is one copy of the evidence available. Copies are not always printed and distributed when the bill comes up for second reading.
In these instances today, all the evidence has been printed and distributed. When a bill is called, it is printed. According to our standing order all bills must be printed before second reading. They have been printed and they meet with our requirements; therefore I can put the question whenever they are called. Theoretically I do not believe hon. members may object on the ground that the evidence has not been printed and distributed. The evidence is not part of the bill.
As I say, I raised the point only as a matter of interest and perhaps as a diversion from the rather monotonous task I was performing of proposing one bill after another. Having done so, hon. members may consider what I have said. It is not a ruling, but I thought I would make these remarks in order to give hon. members an opportunity to think them over. Perhaps on some other occasion I may have to rule, but I want to go further into this myself.

subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: I am not clear as to whether or not you consider it is permissible to refer to the evidence in connection with these cases. May I say that last year there were four or five cases before us which this house refused to accept on the evidence as it came from the other place; we reversed the decision. If we had not been able to refer to this evidence I am sure we would not have managed to win a favourable vote in the house. We have no other information on which to reach a judgment as to whether second reading should be given or refused, except on the basis of the material which is supplied to all hon. members reviewing the work of the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext: I do not want to make a ruling on this point; I have doubts. If the hon. member wishes to continue quoting from the evidence I will not stop him on this occasion.

subtopic: ROSALIE ROSETTI ACASON
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre a question? I was about to ask him whether he would 67509-85

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: GERTRUDE BAILISS GOODLIN
speechtext: Can the hon. member for Skeena, who has been named as the mover of the motion for second reading of this bill, give any reasons why we should support it on second reading?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: GERTRUDE BAILISS GOODLIN
speechtext:
I am particularly pleased that an opportunity has been given to me to express the reason. The hon. member for

Winnipeg North Centre will, 1 think, follow my line of reasoning. If he agrees with me that under certain circumstances, regrettable circumstances, in Canada, it is expedient that people be divorced, then he thinks as I. He and I will both have the greatest respect for those who believe that under no circumstances should couples be divorced.
In this case I, as sponsor of the bill, have reason to believe it can be proved that those circumstances justifying the passing of the bill will be proven or can be proven in our committee. They cannot be proven under the rules, I submit, until such time as the bill reaches the committee which has the power to look into those statements of fact. In other words, sir, the principle of the bill which we are now called upon to approve or disapprove is that if certain facts can be proved, then it is expedient that a divorce be granted. The application of that principle to a particular set of facts cannot be discussed by this house at this time because those facts cannot be made available in final form in this house for the house to take action on them until such time as this house has referred a private bill to a committee.
That is the point on which I was greatly tempted to rise to my feet a few moments ago, because I do feel that that is the basic principle in passing private bills on second reading. I do not know the history, but there has grown up in this parliament the practice of considering this class of private bills differently from others.
It was my privilege at one time to be quite vitally concerned with a contested private bill of another nature which started in the Senate and came to this house. It was most noticeable at that time that no evidence given in the committee of the Senate came to this house. Then there were a number of pipe-line bills a few sessions back which originated in the Senate, and no evidence came to this house upon which it could base approval of the motion for second reading. It was only the basic principle; and whether there was sufficient evidence to make that principle applicable could, I submit, be made known to this house only through the miscellaneous private bills committee or some other appropriate committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: GERTRUDE BAILISS GOODLIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the statement the hon. member for Skeena has made. The fact is that a number of us, including the hon. member, Your Honour and others, will no doubt have private discussions about this matter because it is quite important. It does seem to me, if I may add this word, that what the hon. member for Skeena has said suggests that second reading in the case of divorce bills means something quite 67509-85J

As a member of Your Honour's committee which met for several sessions to deal with the rules and procedures of this house, if I may say so I am pleased with the job we did. C.B.C. DIRECTORATE
speechtext:
1.	Who are the members of the directorate of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation referred to by the minister in the House of Commons on February 7?
2.	How often does the said directorate meet?
3.	What are its duties?
Answer by: Mr. McCann:
On February 1, the hon. member for Eglin-ton asked if there is a directorate in the C.B.C. which concerns itself with whether a program will or will not go on the air. It was thought at the time that the reference was to one of the regular divisions or departments of the C.B.C. The reference and this inquiry is now understood to relate to some presumed special directorate or body that decides whether programs do or do not go on the air.
The C.B.C. advises that there is no such special body which considers and decides whether programs should or should not be
broadcast. The C.B.C. as a corporate entity has full and independent responsibility for all program decisions which are taken through the usual administrative process of chains of responsibility.
